name: Sacubitril/Valsartan
moa: Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin (↑ natriuretic peptides); valsartan blocks AT1 receptor (↓ vasoconstriction/RAAS)
indications: Chronic heart failure to reduce risk of CV death and HF hospitalization (benefits most evident with LVEF below normal — includes HFrEF and many HFpEF per Feb 2021 label expansion); pediatric HF >=1 yr; PARADIGM-HF showed superiority to enalapril in HFrEF
dosing: Usual start 49/51 mg twice daily (BID). Start 24/26 mg BID if not currently taking an ACEi/ARB or previously on low doses (<=10 mg/day enalapril equivalent), severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2), or moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B); then double every 2-4 weeks to target 97/103 mg BID as tolerated; severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) not recommended. Allow a 36-hour washout when switching from an ACEi.
renal: eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2: start 24/26 mg BID (half the usual starting dose); no initial adjustment for eGFR >=30; dialysis: caution (not studied); ARNI-induced hyperkalemia risk with CKD stage 4-5
hepatic: Child-Pugh A: no adjustment; Child-Pugh B: start 24/26 mg BID (half the usual starting dose); Child-Pugh C: not recommended
ades: Hyperkalemia (monitor K+ and creatinine); hypotension; cough (less common than ACEi); angioedema (rare but serious); hyporenal azotemia in CKD
monitoring: K+ and SCr at baseline, 1 week, monthly × 3, then q3 months; BP; eGFR; NYHA class/symptoms
ddi: NSAIDs (↑ renal injury/hyperkalemia); ACEi (contraindicated; do not give within 36 h of the last ACEi dose — angioedema); ARBs (avoid; already contains valsartan); aliskiren (contraindicated in diabetes; avoid if eGFR <60); potassium supplements/K+-sparing agents (↑ hyperkalemia); lithium (↑ levels)
pearls: PARADIGM-HF (2014): reduced mortality/hospitalization vs enalapril. Do NOT use with ACEi/ARB (↑ angioedema risk). K+ monitoring critical. Black box: pregnancy (teratogenic).
trials: PARADIGM-HF, PARAGON-HF, PIONEER-HF
pk: Sacubitril: prodrug → LBQ657 (active) by esterases; t½ sacubitril ~1.4 h, LBQ657 ~11.5 h. Valsartan: t½ ~10 h. Protein binding >94%. Excretion: sacubitril renal 52–68%; valsartan fecal 86%. No CYP interactions.
bbw: PREGNANCY: Can cause fetal harm/death. Discontinue immediately if pregnancy detected.
highyield: Indication expanded (Feb 2021) beyond HFrEF to chronic HF across LVEF range; label states benefits are most clearly evident in patients with LVEF below normal (based on PARAGON-HF), covering HFmrEF and lower-range HFpEF

name: Ivabradine
class: If-Channel Blocker (Hyperpolarization-Activated Cyclic Nucleotide-Gated Channel Inhibitor)
moa: Selective inhibitor of I(f) current in sinoatrial node; slows heart rate via diastolic depolarization (no negative inotropic effect)
indications: Stable symptomatic chronic HFrEF (EF ≤35%) in sinus rhythm with resting HR ≥70 bpm, on maximally tolerated beta-blocker doses (or beta-blocker contraindicated), to reduce the risk of hospitalization for worsening HF (no mortality benefit); SHIFT trial primary outcome (CV death or HF hospitalization) driven by fewer HF hospitalizations; pediatric (≥6 months) stable symptomatic HF due to dilated cardiomyopathy
dosing: PO: 5 mg BID, titrate to target 2.5-7.5 mg BID based on HR (target HR 50-60 bpm); Monitor HR; may need dose reduction if HR <50
renal: No dose adjustment needed; CrCl <15: avoid (limited data)
hepatic: Child-Pugh A/B: no dose adjustment (PK similar to normal; limited experience in B — caution); C: contraindicated
ades: Phosphenes/luminous phenomena (~3% vs 0.5% placebo in SHIFT; transient, usually within first 2 months); bradycardia (~10%); hypertension/BP increase; atrial fibrillation (careful monitoring); conduction abnormalities
monitoring: HR q4 weeks during titration, then q3 months; ECG baseline and after dose changes; visual symptoms (usually resolve)
ddi: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, nefazodone, HIV protease inhibitors) are CONTRAINDICATED (ketoconazole increases AUC ~7-fold); avoid moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors verapamil and diltiazem (also lower HR)
pearls: SHIFT (2010): HR reduction, no mortality benefit but improved HF hospitalizations. Phosphenes (light flashes) common but reversible. Only for SN rhythm (NOT AFib). Bradycardia risk.
trials: SHIFT, SIGNIFY
pk: Distribution t½ ~2 h, effective t½ ~6 h; N-desmethyl metabolite is equipotent (also CYP3A4). Bioavailability ~40% (first-pass). Protein binding 70%. Metabolized by CYP3A4 (major). Excretion: metabolites to a similar extent in feces and urine; ~4% excreted unchanged in urine.
highyield: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors are contraindicated (not dose-reduced); also avoid verapamil/diltiazem (moderate inhibitors that additionally slow HR)

name: Spironolactone
moa: Competitively blocks aldosterone at mineralocorticoid receptor in collecting duct; potassium-sparing diuretic
indications: HFrEF (mortality/hospitalization reduction); primary hyperaldosteronism; resistant hypertension; cirrhosis with ascites
dosing: PO (HFrEF): 12.5-25 mg daily, max 50 mg daily; titrate by K+ tolerance (25 mg every other day if hyperkalemia); RALES trial used 25 mg daily. Other indications use higher doses: HTN 25-100 mg/day; edema/cirrhotic ascites 100 mg/day (up to 400 mg/day in ascites, with furosemide in a 100:40 ratio); primary hyperaldosteronism 100-400 mg/day
renal: eGFR 30-50: consider starting 25 mg every other day (label) and monitor K+ closely; eGFR <30: avoid in HF (guidelines); contraindicated with hyperkalemia; hyperkalemia risk rises steeply as GFR falls
hepatic: Cirrhosis/advanced disease: caution, ↑ risk hyperkalemia; dose adjustment case-by-case
ades: Hyperkalemia (most important; can be life-threatening); gynecomastia (dose-dependent; ~10% at HF doses of 25-50 mg per RALES, higher with doses >150 mg/day; usually reversible after discontinuation); breast tenderness, impotence, menstrual irregularities (antiandrogenic); hyponatremia; worsening renal function
monitoring: K+ and SCr at baseline, day 3, 1 week, 4 weeks, then monthly × 3, then q3 months; BP; eGFR; baseline ECG if K+ >5.5
ddi: ACEi/ARBs/ARNI/NSAIDs/trimethoprim/tacrolimus (↑ hyperkalemia risk); monitor closely; avoid potassium supplements
pearls: RALES (1999): ↓ mortality 30% in HFrEF. Gynecomastia common but reversible after d/c. K+ monitoring is CRITICAL (life-threatening if >6.5). Avoid triple whammy (ACEI/ARB + MRA + NSAID).
trials: RALES, EMPHASIS-HF
pk: Prodrug → active metabolites (canrenone, 7α-thiomethyl spironolactone). t½ ~1.4 h (canrenone ~16.5 h). Protein binding 91%. Extensively metabolized (CYP not major). Excretion: renal (metabolites).
bbw: None. (The former boxed warning for tumorigenicity in chronic rat toxicity studies was removed when Aldactone labeling was converted to PLR format in 2018.)
highyield:
• RALES trial: 30% mortality reduction in severe HFrEF (EF ≤35%)
• Gynecomastia in ~10% men — switch to eplerenone if problematic
• Monitor K⁺ and creatinine at 1 week, 1 month, quarterly
• Hold/reduce if K⁺ >5.5 mEq/L or SCr >2.5 mg/dL

name: Eplerenone
moa: Selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (low affinity for androgen, progesterone, and glucocorticoid receptors minimizes antiandrogenic/hormonal effects); potassium-sparing
indications: HFrEF after acute MI (stable patients with LVEF ≤40% and HF symptoms; EPHESUS); chronic HFrEF NYHA II (EMPHASIS-HF; guideline-supported); hypertension (alone or with other agents)
dosing: PO (HF post-MI): 25 mg daily, titrate to 50 mg daily (target) preferably within 4 weeks (EPHESUS started 3-14 days post-MI); K+ and SCr dependent; max 50 mg daily for HF. HTN: 50 mg daily, may increase to 50 mg BID (max 100 mg/day). With moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors: max 25 mg daily.
renal: CrCl ≤30: contraindicated (all patients); HTN: also contraindicated if CrCl <50 or SCr >2.0 mg/dL (men)/>1.8 mg/dL (women); HF guideline dosing: eGFR 31-49 start 25 mg every other day; hyperkalemia risk
hepatic: No dose adjustment; severe disease: caution
ades: Hyperkalemia (less common than spironolactone due to selectivity); gynecomastia (rare <1%); diarrhea; headache; dizziness
monitoring: K+ and SCr baseline, 3 days, 1 week, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, then periodically; BP; eGFR (label: K+ before start, within first week, and 1 month after start or dose change)
ddi: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, nefazodone, ritonavir, nelfinavir) CONTRAINDICATED; moderate inhibitors (verapamil, diltiazem, erythromycin, saquinavir, fluconazole) require dose limitation (max eplerenone 25 mg/day)
pearls: EMPHASIS-HF (2011, NYHA II chronic HFrEF): reduced CV death/HF hospitalization. EPHESUS (2003, post-MI EF ≤40% with HF): start ~3-14 days post-MI, reduced all-cause mortality. Selective MR binding minimizes gynecomastia vs spironolactone (~1% vs 10-20%).
trials: EPHESUS, EMPHASIS-HF
pk: t½ ~4–6 h. Bioavailability ~69%. Protein binding 49%. Metabolized by CYP3A4. Excretion: renal 67%, fecal 32%.
highyield:
• EPHESUS (post-MI, EF ≤40%): 15% RRR in all-cause mortality (17% RRR in CV death); EMPHASIS-HF (HFrEF, NYHA II): 37% RRR in CV death/HF hospitalization composite (HF hospitalization ↓42%)
• Fewer hormonal side effects than spironolactone (gynecomastia <1%)
• Contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole)
• Contraindicated if K⁺ >5.5 mEq/L at initiation or CrCl ≤30; for HTN also if CrCl <50 or SCr >2.0 (males)/>1.8 (females)

name: Carvedilol
class: Non-Selective Beta-Blocker with Alpha-1 Blocking Activity
moa: Non-selective β1/β2 antagonist + alpha-1 blockade; reduces vasoconstriction and sympathetic tone; reduces cardiac workload
indications: HFrEF (mortality ↓ COPERNICUS, US Carvedilol HF Program, CAPRICORN post-MI); CIBIS = bisoprolol and MERIT-HF = metoprolol succinate, not carvedilol
dosing: PO: 3.125 mg BID, titrate q2 weeks to 6.25, 12.5, 25 mg BID (target); extended-release: 10-80 mg daily
renal: No dose adjustment; caution in severe renal disease
hepatic: Severe hepatic impairment: contraindicated (extensive first-pass metabolism; levels rise markedly); mild-moderate/cirrhosis: caution, consider lower dose
ades: Bradycardia/AV block; hypotension; dizziness (esp. with alpha blockade); fatigue; bronchospasm (non-selective); cold extremities
monitoring: HR, BP q2 weeks during titration; EF at baseline, 3 months; signs of decompensation; SCr/BUN (baseline, periodic)
ddi: Non-dihydropyridine CCB (diltiazem/verapamil): ↑ bradycardia/AV block; clonidine (abrupt d/c ↑ rebound HTN); NSAIDs (↓ efficacy); digoxin (↑ levels)
pearls: Slow titration essential (worsening HF/fluid retention, bradycardia, hypotension/syncope if titrated too rapidly)
trials: COPERNICUS, CAPRICORN, US Carvedilol HF Program, COMET
pk: t½ ~7–10 h. Bioavailability ~25–35% (first-pass; food slows the rate but not the extent of absorption — take with food to ↓ orthostasis). Protein binding ~98%. Metabolized by CYP2D6 and CYP2C9. Excretion: fecal ~60%, renal <2%.
highyield: COPERNICUS and the US Carvedilol HF trials: proven mortality benefit in HFrEF (MERIT-HF was metoprolol succinate, not carvedilol)

name: Metoprolol Succinate
moa: β1-selective adrenergic antagonist at therapeutic doses; reduces HR, contractility, BP; extended-release (ER) for sustained β-blockade
indications: HFrEF (mortality ↓ MERIT-HF); hypertension; angina (labeled Toprol-XL indications); post-MI, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation rate control (off-label for the succinate; post-MI is a labeled indication of metoprolol tartrate)
dosing: HFrEF: start 25 mg once daily (12.5 mg if more severe HF, e.g., NYHA III-IV), titrate q2 weeks (doubling) to target 200 mg once daily (MERIT-HF target and Toprol-XL maximum HF dose). HTN: 25-100 mg once daily (max 400 mg/day); angina: 100 mg once daily (max 400 mg/day)
renal: No dose adjustment; caution CrCl <30
hepatic: Severe disease: caution, reduce dose
ades: Bradycardia; hypotension; fatigue; sexual dysfunction; bronchospasm (less common than non-selective); depression
monitoring: HR, BP q2 weeks during titration; EF; signs of HF decompensation; SCr/BUN periodic
ddi: Diltiazem/verapamil (↑ AV block); clonidine (↑ rebound HTN on d/c); NSAIDs (↓ antihypertensive effect); digoxin (monitor levels)
pearls: MERIT-HF (1999): ↓ mortality 34% in HFrEF. USE SUCCINATE (ER), NOT TARTRATE (immediate-release, less efficacy in HF). Extended-release preferred for HF (better compliance). Cardioselective better tolerated in pulmonary disease vs non-selective.
trials: MERIT-HF (COPERNICUS was a carvedilol trial, not metoprolol succinate)
pk: Extended-release. t½ ~3–7 h. Bioavailability ~50% (first-pass). Protein binding ~12%. Metabolized by CYP2D6 (primary). Excretion: renal ~95% (metabolites).
highyield:
• MERIT-HF: 34% RRR in all-cause mortality vs placebo in HFrEF
• Cardioselective β1 blocker — preferred over carvedilol in reactive airway disease
• Do NOT abruptly discontinue — risk of rebound angina/MI
• CYP2D6 poor metabolizers: higher blood levels; drugs like fluoxetine ↑ levels

name: Digoxin
class: Cardiac Glycoside (Inotropic Agent + AV Node Blocker)
moa: Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → ↑ contractility; also vagomimetic (↑ AV block/bradycardia via vagal stimulation)
indications: HFrEF + AFib with RVR (dual benefit: inotropic + rate control); HF (symptom relief only, no mortality ↓); SVT (particularly adenosine-refractory)
dosing: Load (only if rapid effect needed): 10-15 mcg/kg PO or 8-12 mcg/kg IV total (lean body weight), give 50% initially then 25% q6-8h ×2; Maint: 0.125-0.25 mg daily PO, reduced for renal impairment; adjust by serum digoxin trough concentration (not AUC).
renal: Renally cleared (50-70% unchanged): reduce maintenance dose (e.g., 0.0625-0.125 mg daily or every other day) and loading dose in ESRD; t½ ~3.5-5 days in anuria. Dialysis: not removed by hemodialysis (large Vd ~5-7 L/kg, extensive tissue binding); NO post-dialysis supplemental dose needed.
hepatic: No dose adjustment (only ~13% metabolized; hepatic impairment does not significantly alter PK); HF-related ↓ renal perfusion reduces clearance — dose by renal function and serum levels
ades: Narrow therapeutic index (0.5-2 ng/mL); toxicity: arrhythmias (PACs, PVCs, bigeminy, complete heart block), nausea/vomiting/anorexia, visual disturbances (yellow vision), confusion; hypokalemia (also hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia) worsens toxicity; hyperkalemia is a marker of acute overdose
monitoring: target 0.5-0.9 ng/mL for HF (higher levels associated with increased mortality); ~0.8-2.0 ng/mL range historically for rate control, but keep low end preferred
ddi: Amiodarone (↑ digoxin ~70%; cut digoxin dose 30-50%); verapamil (↑ 50-75%); diltiazem (↑ ~20%); dronedarone (↑ ~2.5-fold; halve dose); thiazide/loop diuretics (↓ K+, ↑ toxicity risk); NSAIDs (↑ levels); amphotericin B (↓ K+); quinidine (↑ digoxin levels 100%)
pearls: DIG trial (1997): no mortality ↓, but ↓ hospitalizations/symptoms in HF. NARROW THERAPEUTIC INDEX = HIGH TOXICITY RISK. K+ hypokalemia critical risk factor. Toxicity mimics arrhythmias/hyperkalemia. Old drug but still useful in HF+AFib. Monitor levels religiously.
trials: DIG Trial, Digitalis Investigation Group
pk: t½ ~36–48 h (renal-dependent). Bioavailability ~70–80% (tablets). Protein binding ~25%. Not metabolized by CYP. Excretion: renal ~50–70% unchanged. Volume of distribution: large (~7 L/kg).
highyield:
• Narrow therapeutic index: target serum level 0.5–0.9 ng/mL for HF (>2 ng/mL = toxicity)
• Toxicity signs: GI (N/V, anorexia), bradyarrhythmias, visual (yellow-green halos), bidirectional VT
• Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypothyroidism all increase toxicity risk
• Not first-line — add-on for rate control in AFib or persistent HF symptoms
• Quinidine, amiodarone, verapamil, spironolactone: all ↑ digoxin levels

name: Amiodarone
class: Class III Antiarrhythmic (Potassium Channel Blocker) + Multi-Channel Effects
moa: K+ channel blockade (Class III: prolongs action potential/refractory period); also Na+ blockade (Class I), β-blockade (Class II), non-selective Ca2+ blockade (Class IV)
indications: Life-threatening recurrent VF and hemodynamically unstable VT (FDA-labeled); off-label/guideline uses: AFib (rate/rhythm control), refractory SVT, cardiomyopathy + arrhythmias, ICD shock reduction, pulseless VF/VT (ACLS)
dosing: IV: pulseless VF/VT (ACLS) 300 mg IV/IO push, then 150 mg; stable VT/AF: 150 mg over 10 min, then 1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min × 18 h (supplemental 150 mg over 10 min for breakthrough); PO: 800-1600 mg daily × 1-3 weeks, then 600-800 daily × 1 month, then 200-400 mg daily (maint; usual 400 mg for ventricular arrhythmias, 100-200 mg for AF)
renal: Minimal renal clearance; dose adjustment minimal; hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4/CYP2C8) dominant
hepatic: Hepatic disease: caution, accumulates; no defined dose adjustment — reduce dose or discontinue if transaminases >3× ULN (or double an elevated baseline); stop if clinical liver injury
ades: Pulmonary toxicity (up to ~17% in some series, fatal in ~10% of cases: pneumonitis, fibrosis, acute dyspnea); hypothyroidism (up to ~10%); hyperthyroidism (~2%); hepatotoxicity; ophthalmic (corneal microdeposits, optic neuritis); photosensitivity; blue-gray skin discoloration; QT prolongation; bradycardia/AV block; peripheral neuropathy
monitoring: Baseline: CXR, PFTs (with DLCO), TFTs, LFTs, ECG; then LFTs and TFTs every 6 months, CXR annually, ECG periodically; PFTs if unexplained cough/dyspnea, CXR abnormality, or clinical suspicion (stop if pulmonary fibrosis); ophthalmic exam at baseline if visual impairment and with visual symptoms (stop if optic neuritis); SCr/K+; QTc interval. Current FDA labeling differs: the amiodarone tablet labeling reviewed in 2024 advises a chest x-ray with history and exam every 3-6 months rather than annually (FDA label, openFDA 2024).
ddi: Warfarin (↑ PT/INR up to ~100% within days; reduce warfarin dose by 1/3 to 1/2); digoxin (↑ levels ~70%; reduce digoxin dose by ~50%); beta-blockers (↑ bradycardia); diltiazem/verapamil (↑ AV block); CYP3A4 substrates (simvastatin [max 20 mg/day], lovastatin [max 40 mg/day], tacrolimus, cyclosporine: ↑ levels); sofosbuvir (symptomatic bradycardia); QT-prolonging drugs (macrolides, fluoroquinolones, azoles: ↑ Torsades risk)
pearls: Most effective antiarrhythmic but HIGHEST toxicity risk. Reserve for life-threatening arrhythmias or when other agents are ineffective/contraindicated (e.g., AF with HFrEF/structural heart disease); do NOT use for asymptomatic arrhythmias. Pulmonary toxicity can be fatal/irreversible (fibrosis); thyroid dysfunction usually manageable. Class III with multi-channel (I, II, IV) effects makes it unique. IV for acute VT/VF. Complex PK (very long half-life, about 58 days on average: steady state takes months without a loading dose). Drug interactions MAJOR.
trials: ARREST, ALIVE, ACLS
pk: t½ extremely long: 40–55 days (range 26–107 days). Bioavailability ~50% (variable). Protein binding >96%. Metabolized by CYP3A4/CYP2C8 → active desethylamiodarone. Excretion: biliary/fecal. Lipophilic — accumulates in tissue.
bbw: PULMONARY TOXICITY (may be fatal). HEPATOTOXICITY (liver failure reported). PROARRHYTHMIA (ventricular arrhythmias). Intended only for life-threatening arrhythmias when alternatives inadequate.
highyield:
• Most potent antiarrhythmic — Vaughan-Williams Class III (also I, II, IV properties)
• Thyroid monitoring mandatory: causes both hypo- and hyperthyroidism (iodine-rich)
• LFTs and TFTs at baseline and every 6 months; CXR at baseline and annually; PFTs at baseline and if symptoms; eye exam if visual impairment or symptoms
• Drug interactions extensive: warfarin (↑ INR; cut warfarin dose 30–50%), digoxin (↑ levels ~70%; halve dose), statins
• Loading phase required due to huge volume of distribution; full effect takes weeks

name: Dronedarone
moa: Multi-channel blockade: K+ (Class III), Na+ (Class I), non-dihydropyridine Ca2+ blocker (Class IV), non-selective beta antagonism (Class II); benzofuran backbone (no iodine)
indications: To reduce risk of hospitalization for AF in patients in sinus rhythm with a history of paroxysmal or persistent AF. CONTRAINDICATED in NYHA Class IV or symptomatic HF with recent decompensation (do NOT use for HFrEF + AFib). Also contraindicated in permanent AF (PALLAS).
dosing: PO: 400 mg twice daily with morning and evening meals (800 mg/day total). No dose-reduced regimen exists; contraindicated in NYHA Class IV HF or NYHA Class II–III HF with recent decompensation (avoid in symptomatic HF).
renal: No dose adjustment (minimal renal excretion); early ~0.1 mg/dL SCr rise from inhibition of tubular creatinine secretion; monitor renal function periodically (true renal failure reported, often with HF)
hepatic: Severe hepatic impairment: contraindicated; moderate: no dose adjustment (limited experience); also contraindicated with prior amiodarone-related liver or lung toxicity
ades: Bradycardia; QT prolongation (Torsades risk ↑ with electrolyte abnormalities); GI upset; asthenia; hepatotoxicity (rare but serious); photosensitivity; neuropathy (less common than amiodarone)
monitoring: Baseline: LFTs, SCr, K+, Mg2+, ECG; then LFTs q6 months; K+/Mg2+ baseline/periodic; HR/BP; QTc interval; symptoms of HF
ddi: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, cyclosporine, nefazodone): CONTRAINDICATED (ketoconazole ↑ dronedarone exposure ~17-fold); moderate inhibitors verapamil/diltiazem (↑ dronedarone ~1.4-1.7×, plus ↑ bradycardia — start low); avoid grapefruit and CYP3A4 inducers; digoxin (↑ ~2.5×; halve dose); dabigatran (↑ levels); simvastatin (max 10 mg/day); warfarin (↑ INR); beta-blockers (↑ AV block); QT-prolonging drugs incl. class I/III antiarrhythmics (contraindicated); potassium-depleting diuretics (hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia ↑ Torsades)
pearls: ATHENA: ↓ CV hospitalization/death in non-permanent AF (no clear all-cause mortality benefit). ANDROMEDA: ↑ mortality in symptomatic HF → contraindication. PALLAS: harm in permanent AF (stopped early).
trials: ATHENA, ANDROMEDA, PALLAS, DIONYSOS, EURIDIS/ADONIS
pk: t½ ~13–19 h. Bioavailability ~4% fasted, ~15% with a high-fat meal (take with meals). Protein binding >98%. Metabolized by CYP3A4. Excretion: fecal ~84%, renal ~6%.
bbw: CONTRAINDICATED in NYHA Class IV or decompensated HF (doubled mortality in ANDROMEDA). CONTRAINDICATED in permanent AFib (increased CV mortality, stroke, HF hospitalization in PALLAS).
highyield:
• Non-iodinated analog of amiodarone — fewer thyroid/pulmonary side effects
• ATHENA: reduced AFib hospitalization, but NO mortality benefit
• Causes SCr elevation (~0.1 mg/dL) via tubular secretion inhibition — not true renal decline
• Contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and Class I/III antiarrhythmics
• Do NOT use in permanent AFib — PALLAS trial stopped early for harm

name: Sotalol
moa: K+ channel (IKr) blockade (Class III: prolongs action potential duration) + non-selective beta-1/2 blockade (Class II, l-isomer); significant beta-blockade occurs at low doses (≥25 mg), whereas Class III effects become significant only at ≥160 mg/day
indications: Documented life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias (e.g., sustained VT); maintenance of normal sinus rhythm in symptomatic AFib/AFL (rhythm control, not rate control; avoid in minimally symptomatic AF); SVT (off-label)
dosing: PO: 80 mg BID (interval adjusted for CrCl), increase by 80 mg/day every 3 days if QTc <500 ms; AF: usually 120 mg BID (max 160 mg BID); ventricular: 160-320 mg/day in divided doses (480-640 mg/day for refractory arrhythmias); IV sotalol (sotalol hydrochloride injection) for initiation/substitution when oral not possible (Sotylize is an oral solution, not IV)
renal: CRITICAL (renally eliminated unchanged; 2024 course): AF maintenance: CrCl >60: q12h; CrCl 40-60: q24h; CrCl <40: contraindicated. Ventricular arrhythmias: CrCl >60: q12h; CrCl 30-60: q24h; CrCl 10-30: q36-48h; CrCl <10: individualize. Dialysis: partly removed; no specific dosing recommendation. Current FDA labeling differs: current Betapace/Betapace AF labeling (2024) uses one extended-interval schedule for all indications (CrCl 30-59 q24h, 10-29 q36-48h, <10 individualize) and no longer lists CrCl <40 as an AF contraindication (FDA label, 2024).
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment; use caution
ades: QT prolongation (Torsades de Pointes risk ↑ with hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia); bradycardia; hypotension; fatigue; sexual dysfunction; bronchospasm (non-selective beta-blockade, esp. in COPD/asthma)
monitoring: Baseline ECG (QTc), K+ (keep ≥4), Mg2+, SCr/CrCl, BUN; QTc 2-4 h after each dose during initiation/up-titration (keep QTc <500 ms); HR <50-55 BPM: caution; hypokalemia (K+ <4) or hypomagnesemia: risk factor for Torsades; EF (baseline, periodic); symptoms of arrhythmia
ddi: QT-prolonging drugs (macrolides, antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones, domperidone: ↑ Torsades); hypokalemia-inducing agents (loop diuretics, thiazide, amphotericin: ↑ Torsades); NSAIDs (↓ efficacy); anti-arrhythmics (additive effects, caution)
pearls: Non-selective beta-blocker (bronchospasm risk; contraindicated in bronchial asthma). SEVERE Torsades risk if QTc >500 ms or K+ deranged. Renal clearance dependent = MAJOR DOSE ADJUSTMENT in CKD. Less extracardiac organ toxicity than amiodarone. AF: contraindicated if CrCl <40 mL/min. Do NOT start for AF if baseline QTc >450 ms (no sex-specific cutoff in the label).
trials: ESVEM, SWORD
pk: t½ ~12 h. Bioavailability ~90–100%. Protein binding minimal (<10%). NOT metabolized by liver/CYP. Excretion: renal ~80% unchanged (adjust for CrCl).
bbw: PROARRHYTHMIA: Life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias (TdP) with QT prolongation. Initiate/re-initiate (and up-titrate) in a facility with continuous ECG monitoring and resuscitation capability for ≥3 days; calculate CrCl to set the dosing interval; if QTc ≥500 ms, reduce dose, lengthen interval, or stop.
highyield:
• Class III antiarrhythmic + non-selective β-blocker (Class II)
• Dose-dependent QT prolongation — monitor QTc and electrolytes
• Renal interval: AF CrCl 40–60 q24h, <40 contraindicated; ventricular CrCl 30–60 q24h, 10–30 q36–48h
• Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia dramatically increase TdP risk — correct before use

name: Ticagrelor
moa: Reversible binding to P2Y12 ADP receptor on platelets; active metabolite contributes; faster onset (1 h) and offset (3-5 days) vs clopidogrel
indications: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS: STEMI/NSTEMI/UA) or history of MI to reduce CV death/MI/stroke (PLATO showed superiority to clopidogrel for the first 12 months; PEGASUS beyond 1 year); post-PCI stent (12 months); CAD at high risk without prior MI/stroke (THEMIS, established in T2DM — not PLATO-based); acute ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤5) or high-risk TIA (THALES)
dosing: PO: 180 mg loading (ACS), then 90 mg BID for the first 12 months after ACS; after 1 year reduce to 60 mg BID for long-term secondary prevention (PEGASUS regimen). CAD without prior MI/stroke: 60 mg BID. Stroke/TIA: 180 mg load, then 90 mg BID for up to 30 days. Give with aspirin 75-100 mg/day.
renal: No dose adjustment; severe renal impairment (eGFR <30): caution (increased bleeding risk)
hepatic: Avoid if severe hepatic disease (no data)
ades: Bleeding (↑ vs clopidogrel in PLATO, but offset by ↓ CV deaths); bradycardia (2-3%, vagal, often asymptomatic); dyspnea (~14% in PLATO/PEGASUS, up to 21% in THEMIS; usually mild, often resolves); bradyarrhythmias (AV block rare); gout (hyperuricemia)
monitoring: Baseline CBC, INR (if on warfarin); assess for signs of bleeding; HR (bradycardia); ECG if bradycardic symptoms; renal function; liver function; symptoms of dyspnea
ddi: Warfarin/anticoagulants (↑ bleeding, though used together in some trials); aspirin >100 mg/day (↓ ticagrelor efficacy, use ≤100 mg/day); NSAIDs (↑ bleeding); strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, voriconazole) and strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin): AVOID; simvastatin/lovastatin >40 mg/day not recommended; digoxin (monitor levels); opioids (delay/↓ absorption)
pearls: PLATO (2009): ↓ CV death/MI vs clopidogrel in ACS. Reversible (advantage over prasugrel/clopidogrel). Bradycardia common but usually asymptomatic. Dyspnea (~14%): tolerable, reversible. Faster onset/offset than clopidogrel. NO genetic testing needed (vs clopidogrel CYP2C19). Bleeding risk ↑ vs clopidogrel but offset by clinical benefit.
trials: PLATO, PEGASUS-TIMI 54
pk: t½ ~7–8.5 h (active metabolite ~8.5 h). Bioavailability ~36%. Protein binding >99%. Metabolized by CYP3A4 (major). Excretion: fecal ~58%, renal ~26%.
bbw: BLEEDING RISK: Can cause significant and fatal bleeding. Avoid in patients with active bleeding, prior ICH. Maintain aspirin dose ≤100 mg/day (higher doses reduce effectiveness).
highyield:
• Does NOT require hepatic activation (unlike clopidogrel/prasugrel) — faster, more consistent effect
• PLATO trial: superior to clopidogrel in ACS (reduced CV death, MI, stroke)
• Dyspnea in ~14% (adenosine-mediated) — usually transient, not bronchospasm
• Hold 5 days before CABG; no specific reversal agent — platelet transfusion did not reverse the effect and is unlikely to help (circulating drug inhibits transfused platelets)
• Aspirin dose >100 mg/day reduces ticagrelor efficacy — keep aspirin ≤81 mg

name: Prasugrel
moa: Irreversible P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonist (thienopyridine); active metabolite is potent/fast (peak 30 min); stronger antiplatelet effect vs clopidogrel
indications: ACS (STEMI/NSTEMI) with PCI planned; post-PCI stent placement; TRITON-TIMI 38 showed ↓ stent thrombosis vs clopidogrel (but ↑ bleeding)
dosing: PO: 60 mg loading dose (single dose for all patients), then 10 mg once daily maintenance. For weight <60 kg, consider reducing maintenance to 5 mg daily. Generally not recommended in age ≥75 (except high-risk diabetics/prior MI). DAPT × 12 months.
renal: No dose adjustment; end-stage renal disease (eGFR <15): limited data, caution
hepatic: Mild-moderate (Child-Pugh A/B): no dose adjustment; severe: not studied — caution (higher bleeding risk)
ades: Bleeding (↑ vs clopidogrel, especially if age ≥75 or weight <60 kg, TRITON showed ↑ major bleed); bradycardia (rare); rash; thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP: extremely rare)
monitoring: CBC baseline (platelet count); assess for signs of bleeding; renal function; liver function; symptoms of arrhythmia; consider HAS-BLED score
ddi: Anticoagulants/warfarin (↑ bleeding); aspirin >100 mg daily (↑ bleeding); NSAIDs (↑ bleeding); opioids (may ↓ prasugrel absorption/efficacy, mechanism unclear)
pearls: TRITON-TIMI 38 (2007): ↓ stent thrombosis vs clopidogrel, but ↑ major bleeding (esp. fatal bleeding and bleeding needing transfusion). Irreversible (7-10 day recovery once d/c). Stronger platelet inhibition = ↑ efficacy but ↑ bleeding. Age ≥75 or weight <60 kg: higher bleeding risk (use 5 mg). Opioid paradox: may reduce absorption (use before PCI or post-PCI post-opioid). NO genetic testing (vs clopidogrel CYP2C19).
trials: TRITON-TIMI 38, TRILOGY ACS, ACCOAST
pk: Prodrug → active metabolite by esterases + CYP3A4/CYP2B6. t½ active metabolite ~7 h. Bioavailability ~79% (prodrug). Protein binding active metabolite ~98%. Excretion: urine ~68%, fecal ~27%.
bbw: BLEEDING RISK: Can cause significant and fatal bleeding. CONTRAINDICATED in patients with active pathological bleeding or prior TIA or stroke. Generally not recommended in age ≥75 (except high-risk: diabetes or prior MI). Do not start if urgent CABG likely; stop ≥7 days before surgery. Additional bleeding risk factors: weight <60 kg (consider 5 mg), propensity to bleed, concomitant anticoagulants/fibrinolytics/chronic NSAIDs.
highyield:
• TRITON-TIMI 38: superior to clopidogrel in STEMI/ACS-PCI; but ↑ major bleeding
• Irreversible P2Y12 inhibitor — hold 7 days before CABG
• Absolute contraindication: prior stroke/TIA (net harm shown in TRITON-TIMI 38)
• Preferred over clopidogrel in STEMI (faster activation, no non-responders)
• No dose adjustment needed for renal impairment

name: Clopidogrel
moa: Irreversible P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonist; PRODRUG (requires hepatic CYP2C19 activation); peak antiplatelet effect 3-7 days
indications: Acute coronary syndrome (NSTEMI, STEMI with thrombolysis); post-PCI stent (BMS: 1 month; DES: 12 months); stable CAD; secondary prevention post-MI/stroke; PAD
dosing: PO: 300-600 mg loading (ACS/PCI), then 75 mg daily maintenance; DAPT: 12 months typical post-ACS (with aspirin 81-100 mg daily)
renal: No dose adjustment; ESRD: caution
hepatic: Hepatic disease: reduced activation; severe: avoid or careful monitoring
ades: Bleeding (GI bleeding most common; PPIs lower GI-bleed risk — choose pantoprazole); rash; neutropenia (rare, 0.04%); TTP (rare, 1-2 per million); hypersensitivity; Stevens-Johnson; toxic epidermal necrolysis (very rare)
monitoring: CBC baseline (if symptoms: fever/jaundice assess for TTP); assess for bleeding signs; check CYP2C19 genotype (if available/useful); PPI use assess (omeprazole/esomeprazole ↓ efficacy); symptoms of arrhythmia
ddi: Omeprazole/esomeprazole (CYP2C19 inhibition ↓ active metabolite — avoid; pantoprazole preferred if a PPI is needed); other strong/moderate CYP2C19 inhibitors (fluconazole, fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, voriconazole, ticlopidine): avoid; repaglinide (clopidogrel glucuronide inhibits CYP2C8 — avoid or limit); opioids (delay/↓ absorption); anticoagulants/NSAIDs/SSRIs (↑ bleeding). H2-blockers: cimetidine (a CYP2C19 inhibitor) may reduce clopidogrel activation; famotidine is preferred. Ranitidine does not significantly affect clopidogrel and was withdrawn from the US market in 2020.
pearls: Decades-old standard for ACS/stents. PRODRUG: CYP2C19 dependent (genetic polymorphisms affect response; poor metabolizers respond minimally). PPI interactions: omeprazole/esomeprazole problematic (↓ activation); pantoprazole preferred. Irreversible (7-10 day recovery). Slower onset than prasugrel/ticagrelor (peak 3-7 days). TTP/hematologic toxicity rare but serious (fever/jaundice: urgent CBC). Alternative: switch to ticagrelor/prasugrel if poor response.
trials: CURE, COMMIT, CAPRIE
pk: Prodrug → active metabolite by CYP2C19 (major) + CYP3A4. t½ active metabolite ~30 min. Parent t½ ~6 h. Protein binding ~98%. Excretion: urine ~50%, fecal ~46%.
bbw: DIMINISHED EFFICACY IN CYP2C19 POOR METABOLIZERS: Reduced platelet inhibition. Consider alternative for high-risk patients.
highyield: CYP2C19 poor metabolizers (~2-4% of Whites/Blacks, up to ~14% in East Asians) have reduced efficacy

name: Rivaroxaban
moa: Selective direct Factor Xa inhibition (both free and prothrombinase-bound); does not require antithrombin; ↓ prothrombin generation
indications: NVAF stroke/systemic embolism prevention; DVT/PE treatment and reduction in risk of recurrence; VTE prophylaxis after hip/knee replacement and in acutely ill medical patients; chronic CAD/PAD risk reduction with aspirin (rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BID; COMPASS; incl. after lower-extremity revascularization); pediatric VTE treatment and thromboprophylaxis after Fontan. (The ACS indication [ATLAS ACS 2-TIMI 51] is not FDA-approved in the US.)
dosing: AF stroke prevention: 20 mg once daily with the evening meal; reduce to 15 mg once daily if CrCl ≤50 mL/min (incl. ESRD on dialysis). VTE treatment: 15 mg BID with food × 21 days, then 20 mg once daily with food; after ≥6 months, 10 mg daily for extended prevention. Hip/knee replacement: 10 mg daily × 35/12 days. Acutely ill medical: 10 mg daily × 31-39 days. CAD/PAD: 2.5 mg BID + aspirin 75-100 mg.
renal: NVAF: CrCl 15-50 (and ESRD on dialysis): 15 mg daily (CrCl <30 not studied; PK-based); VTE treatment: avoid if CrCl <=30; CAD/PAD: no adjustment; significant renal impairment ↑ AUC. Current FDA labeling differs: current Xarelto labeling permits VTE treatment and prophylaxis down to CrCl 15 mL/min and advises avoiding use only below 15 (FDA label).
hepatic: Child-Pugh A: no change; Child-Pugh B-C (or any hepatic disease with coagulopathy): avoid
ades: Bleeding (major: 2-3.6% annually in AF, comparable to warfarin); GI bleed (↑ risk); intracranial hemorrhage; hematuria; epistaxis; dyspepsia; rash
monitoring: Baseline: CBC, PT/INR (not monitored on DOAC typically), renal function, LFTs; periodic renal function (yearly or if AKI risk); assess bleeding signs; adherence (no monitoring levels required)
ddi: Combined P-gp + strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, lopinavir/ritonavir): ↑ rivaroxaban levels — avoid; combined P-gp + strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort): ↓ efficacy — avoid; NSAIDs/aspirin (↑ bleeding); other anticoagulants (↑ bleeding; avoid concomitant use); antiplatelet agents (↑ bleeding risk)
pearls: ROCKET-AF (2011): non-inferior to warfarin for AF stroke prevention. Once-daily (with food) = convenience. Hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4, P-gp substrate). Reversal: andexanet alfa (Andexxa; FDA-approved 2018 for both rivaroxaban and apixaban life-threatening bleeding) or 4F-PCC. GI absorption food-dependent for 15/20 mg: MUST take with food (↓ absorption fasting; 10 mg food-independent). Peak levels 2-4h. Half-life 5-13h. Direct Xa inhibition (fast, predictable). Anticoagulation monitoring NOT required.
trials: ROCKET-AF, EINSTEIN, COMPASS
pk: t½ ~5–9 h (young), ~11–13 h (elderly). Bioavailability: 15 mg/20 mg tablets 80% with food (take WITH FOOD for ≥15 mg). Protein binding 92–95%. Metabolized by CYP3A4/CYP2J2 + P-gp substrate. Excretion: urine ~66% (36% unchanged), feces ~28% (7% unchanged).
bbw: PREMATURE DISCONTINUATION INCREASES STROKE RISK (AFib): Do not stop without adequate anticoagulation. SPINAL/EPIDURAL HEMATOMA: Risk with neuraxial procedures.
highyield: Andexanet alfa (Andexxa) is the FDA-approved specific factor Xa reversal agent for rivaroxaban/apixaban life-threatening bleeding; 4-factor PCC is the alternative. Updated after the 2024 course: Andexxa was voluntarily withdrawn from the US market effective Dec 22, 2025 after an FDA safety communication on thromboembolic risk (ANNEXA-I), leaving 4F-PCC as the practical reversal option (FDA/AstraZeneca, 2025). Updated after the 2024 course: Andexxa withdrawn from the US market Dec 2025.

name: Apixaban
class: Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) — direct Factor Xa inhibitor
moa: Selective, reversible, direct inhibitor of Factor Xa (free and prothrombinase-bound). Prevents conversion of prothrombin to thrombin → anticoagulation. Does NOT inhibit thrombin directly (unlike dabigatran). Predictable pharmacokinetics.
indications: NVAF stroke/systemic embolism prevention; DVT prophylaxis after hip/knee replacement; DVT/PE treatment; reduction in risk of recurrent DVT/PE following initial therapy. NOT FDA-approved for VTE prophylaxis in acutely ill medical patients (ADOPT failed to show benefit and increased major bleeding; APEX studied betrixaban, not apixaban).
dosing: NVAF: 5 mg BID; reduce to 2.5 mg BID if 2 of 3: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, SCr ≥1.5 mg/dL. DVT/PE treatment: 10 mg BID x 7 days → 5 mg BID. Extended VTE prophylaxis: 2.5 mg BID. Post-surgery: 2.5 mg BID.
renal: NVAF: reduce to 2.5 mg BID only if ≥2 of: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, SCr ≥1.5 mg/dL. ESRD on hemodialysis: 5 mg BID, or 2.5 mg BID if age ≥80 OR weight ≤60 kg (FDA label, based on a single-dose pharmacokinetic study in 8 ESRD subjects on hemodialysis [Wang 2016]; the 2014 label change predates RENAL-AF, which was terminated early and did not establish efficacy/safety in this population). VTE treatment/prophylaxis: no renal dose adjustment.
hepatic: Avoid in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C). No dose adjustment for mild-moderate. Caution in moderate hepatic impairment.
ades: Bleeding (major GI bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage — GI bleeding rate similar to warfarin; ICH rate lower than warfarin). Anemia, bruising. No hepatotoxicity signal.
monitoring: Standard: clinical assessment for bleeding. No routine level monitoring required. Anti-Xa activity level for special situations (extremes of weight, renal impairment, suspicion of subtherapeutic dosing, perioperative decisions). CBC, SCr q6–12 months (renal function for dosing decisions).
ddi: P-gp AND CYP3A4 substrate (dual pathway — fewer interactions than some DOACs). P-gp + CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir — increase apixaban levels significantly; reduce dose by 50% if on 5 or 10 mg BID; avoid if already on 2.5 mg BID). P-gp + CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin — decrease apixaban levels ≥50% — avoid combination). Avoid other anticoagulants/dual antiplatelet.
pearls: ARISTOTLE trial: apixaban superior to warfarin for NVAF (lower stroke, ICH, mortality, bleeding). Better safety profile than warfarin (especially ICH). REVERSAL: andexanet alfa (Andexxa) specifically reverses anti-Xa DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban). Andexanet alfa approved for life-threatening bleeding. PERIOPERATIVE MANAGEMENT: hold 1–2 days before low-bleed-risk procedures; 3–5 days for high-bleed-risk procedures depending on renal function. No bridging required for most cases. SPECIAL NOTE: apixaban 2.5 mg BID dose HALF DOSE — do not confuse with full 5 mg BID dose.
trials: ARISTOTLE (NVAF), AMPLIFY (VTE treatment), AMPLIFY-EXT (extended VTE prevention), ADVANCE-1/2/3 (post-orthopedic VTE prophylaxis)
pk: t½ ~12 h. Bioavailability ~50% (not food-dependent for ≤10 mg). Protein binding 87%. Metabolized by CYP3A4/P-gp. Excretion: fecal ~56%, renal ~27%.
bbw: PREMATURE DISCONTINUATION INCREASES STROKE RISK (AFib). SPINAL/EPIDURAL HEMATOMA: Risk with neuraxial anesthesia/spinal puncture.
highyield: Andexanet alfa (Andexxa) is the specific FDA-approved reversal agent for apixaban (and rivaroxaban) life-threatening bleeding; 4-factor PCC (Kcentra) is the alternative. Updated after the 2024 course: Andexxa was voluntarily withdrawn from the US market effective Dec 22, 2025 after an FDA safety communication on thromboembolic risk (ANNEXA-I), leaving 4F-PCC as the practical reversal option (FDA/AstraZeneca, 2025). Updated after the 2024 course: Andexxa was withdrawn from the US market Dec 2025; for the exam still know it as the factor Xa-inhibitor reversal agent.

name: Edoxaban
moa: Selective direct Factor Xa inhibition (prothrombinase-bound Xa preferentially); once-daily dosing; rapid absorption
indications: AFib stroke prevention (ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48: non-inferiority vs warfarin; do not use if CrCl >95); DVT/PE treatment after 5-10 days of initial parenteral anticoagulant (HOKUSAI-VTE). Post-op thromboprophylaxis is NOT a US-approved indication.
dosing: AF: 60 mg daily; reduce to 30 mg daily only if CrCl 15-50. (Weight ≤60 kg and select P-gp inhibitors trigger 30 mg only for VTE treatment, not AF.)
renal: CrCl 15-50: 30 mg daily for AF; CrCl <15: avoid; significant renal clearance (50%) means CKD adjustment important
hepatic: Child-Pugh A: no adjustment; Child-Pugh B or C: not recommended (intrinsic coagulation abnormalities)
ades: Bleeding (major: 2.7% annually for AF, similar to warfarin); GI bleed; intracranial hemorrhage; hematuria; dyspepsia; rash
monitoring: Baseline: CBC, renal function, LFTs; periodic renal function (yearly if CKD); bleeding assessment; drug interactions (P-gp); adherence (once-daily = easier)
ddi: P-gp inhibitors (verapamil, quinidine, short-term azithromycin/clarithromycin/erythromycin, oral itraconazole/ketoconazole: ↑ edoxaban; reduce to 30 mg only for VTE treatment — no adjustment in NVAF); P-gp inducers (rifampin: avoid; St. John's Wort: ↓ efficacy); NSAIDs/aspirin (↑ bleeding); anticoagulants (↑ bleeding); antiplatelet agents (↑ bleeding)
pearls: ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (2013): non-inferiority to warfarin for AFib. Once-daily dosing (convenience). High renal clearance (50%) = dose adjustment in CKD (30 mg daily if CrCl 15-50). P-gp substrate (food/drug interactions). NO reversal agent approved (unlike apixaban andexanet alfa). Lower prevalence among prescribers vs apixaban/rivaroxaban. Peak levels 1-2h. Half-life 10-14h. Fast absorption. Less bleeding vs warfarin in ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48.
trials: ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48, HOKUSAI-VTE
pk: t½ ~10–14 h. Bioavailability ~62% (not significantly food-affected). Protein binding 55%. Minimal CYP metabolism; P-gp substrate. Excretion: renal ~50%, biliary ~50%.
bbw: REDUCED EFFICACY AT HIGHER CrCl: Avoid in non-valvular AFib if CrCl >95 mL/min (increased ischemic stroke vs warfarin in ENGAGE AF). PREMATURE DISCONTINUATION: ↑ ischemic event (stroke) risk. SPINAL/EPIDURAL HEMATOMA: risk with neuraxial anesthesia/spinal puncture.
highyield: No FDA-approved specific reversal agent for edoxaban; 4-factor PCC is the recommended option (andexanet alfa was approved only for apixaban/rivaroxaban). Updated after the 2024 course: andexanet (Andexxa) was withdrawn from the US market Dec 22, 2025 (FDA/AstraZeneca, 2025). Updated after the 2024 course: Andexxa withdrawn from the US market Dec 2025.

name: Dabigatran
moa: Selective direct thrombin (Factor II) inhibition; reversibly binds to thrombin active site; does not require antithrombin
indications: AFib stroke prevention (RE-LY: 150 mg BID superior to warfarin); DVT/PE treatment after 5-10 days parenteral anticoagulation and reduction in risk of recurrence; DVT/PE prophylaxis after hip replacement surgery; pediatric VTE. Not indicated for ACS/stents; contraindicated with mechanical heart valves (RE-ALIGN).
dosing: AF: 150 mg BID (CrCl >30); 75 mg BID if CrCl 15-30, or CrCl 30-50 with dronedarone or systemic ketoconazole (US label; age ≥80 is not a US dose-reduction criterion); DVT/PE: 150 mg BID after 5-10 days parenteral anticoagulation (CrCl >30); hip replacement prophylaxis: 110 mg on day 1, then 220 mg once daily × 28-35 days
renal: NVAF: CrCl 15-30: 75 mg BID; CrCl <15 or dialysis: not recommended; VTE treatment/prophylaxis: avoid if CrCl ≤30; significant renal clearance (80%); dialyzable
hepatic: Child-Pugh A: no change; B-C: caution/avoid
ades: Bleeding (major ~3.1%/yr with 150 mg BID vs ~3.4%/yr warfarin in RE-LY; ICH ↓ vs warfarin; GI bleeding ↑ vs warfarin); dyspepsia/gastritis-like symptoms (~35%); intracranial hemorrhage; hematuria; epistaxis; gastritis
monitoring: Baseline: CBC, renal function, LFTs; renal function q3-12 months (esp. age ≥75 or CKD); assess bleeding signs; drug interactions (P-gp); GI symptoms (dyspepsia)
ddi: P-gp inhibitors (verapamil, dronedarone, clarithromycin, ritonavir: ↑ dabigatran, caution); P-gp inducers (rifampin, St. John's Wort: ↓ efficacy, avoid); NSAIDs/aspirin (↑ bleeding); anticoagulants (↑ bleeding); weak acid reducers (H2-blockers, PPIs: may ↓ absorption slightly)
pearls: RE-LY (2009): SUPERIOR to warfarin (↓ stroke/systemic embolism ~35% with 150 mg BID; major bleeding similar to warfarin, ↓ ICH). DTI (not Xa inhibitor). BID dosing (inconvenience). High renal clearance (80%) = CKD dose adjustments critical. Capsules contain tartaric acid (pellets inside, not tablets) = swallow whole, do NOT open (↑ bleeding). GI bleeding risk ↑ vs warfarin but offset by ↓ hemorrhagic stroke/mortality. Idarucizumab (reversal agent) available, monoclonal antibody (effective reversal). Peak levels 1-3h. Half-life 12-17h.
trials: RE-LY, RE-COVER, RE-MEDY
pk: Prodrug (dabigatran etexilate) → active dabigatran via esterases. t½ ~12–17 h. Bioavailability ~6–7% (low but consistent). Protein binding 35%. NOT a CYP substrate. P-gp substrate. Excretion: renal ~80% unchanged.
bbw: PREMATURE DISCONTINUATION INCREASES STROKE RISK (AFib). SPINAL/EPIDURAL HEMATOMA risk with neuraxial procedures.
highyield:
• Specific reversal agent idarucizumab (Praxbind, 5 g IV) — dabigatran-specific antidote
• Take with glass of water; do NOT crush/chew capsules (pellets irritate GI); GI upset common — take with food
• RE-LY trial: non-inferior (110 mg) or superior (150 mg) to warfarin in AFib
• Renal: avoid if CrCl <15 (NVAF) or ≤30 (VTE); reduce to 75 mg BID if CrCl 15–30 (NVAF); P-gp inhibitors: avoid if CrCl <30 (NVAF) or <50 (VTE); dronedarone/ketoconazole with CrCl 30–50 → 75 mg BID (NVAF)
• Dronedarone and ketoconazole (P-gp inhibitors): ↑ dabigatran levels significantly

name: Warfarin
moa: Inhibits vitamin K-dependent carboxylation (Factors II, VII, IX, X, proteins C & S); prevents γ-carboxylation in liver; requires 3-5 days for full effect (delayed until vitamin K-dependent factors eliminated)
indications: AFib (stroke prevention); VTE (DVT/PE acute & secondary prevention); mechanical heart valves (indefinite); thrombophilia; post-MI with LV thrombus; recurrent thrombotic events
dosing: PO: usual initial dose 2-5 mg daily (5 mg typical; ≤2.5 mg if elderly/frail, liver disease, HF, interacting drugs; 10 mg × 2 days is an option in healthy VTE outpatients per CHEST; large loading doses not recommended), then 2-10 mg daily (adjusted by INR); target INR 2-3 (most indications, incl. mechanical bileaflet aortic valve without risk factors), 2.5-3.5 (mechanical mitral valve or aortic valve with risk factors); requires frequent INR monitoring
renal: No dose adjustment; prolonged INR if severe renal impairment
hepatic: Liver disease: ↑ INR risk, reduce dose; avoid in decompensated cirrhosis
ades: Bleeding (most common; major/fatal incl. ICH, GI); skin necrosis (early in therapy, protein C deficiency); purple toe syndrome/systemic cholesterol microembolization; calciphylaxis; alopecia; teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy). Warfarin does not cause HIT; however, initiating warfarin during acute untreated HIT can precipitate venous limb gangrene/skin necrosis.
monitoring: INR baseline, 3-5 days post-initiation, then q2-4 weeks until stable, then q4-12 weeks; PT/INR therapeutic monitoring MANDATORY; dietary vitamin K (dietary consistency important: affects INR); signs of bleeding; hepatic/renal function baseline
ddi: NSAIDs/aspirin (↑ bleeding); phenytoin (↓ warfarin levels); rifampin (↑ metabolism, ↓ INR); antibiotics (macrolides, fluoroquinolones, TMP-SMX: ↑ INR); antifungals (azoles: ↑ INR); amiodarone (↑ INR significantly); SSRIs (↑ INR); statins (↑ INR); alcohol (chronic: ↓ INR); vitamin K supplements (↓ INR)
pearls: Decades-old standard, still used for mechanical valves & select cases. NARROW THERAPEUTIC INDEX: INR monitoring MANDATORY (requires regular blood draws, patient education on vitamin K diet). Slow onset (3-5 days, bridge with LMWH or UFH acutely). Many drug interactions. Pregnancy contraindicated (teratogenic). Supratherapeutic INR without bleeding: hold ± oral vitamin K (phytonadione) if INR >10; major bleeding: 4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K 5-10 mg (FFP only if PCC unavailable). Dietary vitamin K affects INR (patient education critical). DOACs preferred over warfarin for most AFib, but warfarin still indicated for mechanical valves.
trials: AFFIRM, CHEST Guidelines
pk: Racemic mixture: S-warfarin (3–4× more potent, CYP2C9) + R-warfarin (CYP1A2, CYP3A4). t½ ~36–42 h. Bioavailability ~93–100%. Protein binding ~99%. Excretion: renal ~92% (metabolites).
bbw: BLEEDING RISK: May cause major or fatal bleeding. Risk factors: high INR, age ≥65, variable INR, prior GI bleed, hypertension, cerebrovascular disease, anemia. Regular INR monitoring required.
highyield:
• Vitamin K antagonist — inhibits factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C, S (onset 2–3 days)
• Reversal: Vitamin K (slow), FFP (faster), 4-factor PCC (fastest for emergent reversal)
• Drug interactions: CYP2C9 inhibitors ↑ INR (fluconazole, amiodarone, metronidazole); inducers ↓ INR (rifampin, carbamazepine)
• Pharmacogenomics: CYP2C9 and VKORC1 polymorphisms affect dose requirements significantly
• Target INR 2–3 for most indications; 2.5–3.5 for mechanical mitral valve

name: Alteplase (tPA)
moa: Recombinant human tPA; binds fibrin in thrombus → converts plasminogen to plasmin → dissolves fibrin clot. Fibrin-selective (activated mainly in presence of clot-bound plasminogen). Dose-dependent systemic lytic state also occurs.
indications: Acute ischemic stroke: within 3 h of symptom onset (FDA label); extended to 3–4.5 h in eligible patients per AHA/ASA guidelines (the original ECASS III exclusions — age >80, oral anticoagulant use, NIHSS >25, prior stroke plus diabetes — are no longer absolute per 2019 AHA/ASA guidance); acute STEMI (when timely PCI unavailable); acute massive PE; Cathflo Activase: restoring function of occluded central venous access devices
dosing: Ischemic stroke: 0.9 mg/kg IV (max 90 mg); 10% as IV bolus over 1 min, remaining 90% over 60 min. Begin within 3h of onset (label); can extend to 4.5h in selected patients per guidelines. STEMI (accelerated, >67 kg): 15 mg bolus, 50 mg over 30 min, then 35 mg over 60 min (≤67 kg: 15 mg, then 0.75 mg/kg [max 50 mg], then 0.5 mg/kg [max 35 mg]); max 100 mg. Massive PE: 100 mg IV over 2h. Cathflo: 2 mg instilled into the occluded lumen, may repeat once.
renal: No dose adjustment (hepatically cleared; minimal renal effect).
hepatic: No specific adjustment; severe disease: caution (↑ bleeding risk)
ades: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH: 6% stroke, 0.4% STEMI); major bleeding (GI, pulmonary, retroperitoneal); reperfusion arrhythmias (STEMI, bradycardia, asystole); myocardial rupture (post-MI, rare); fever; nausea
monitoring: Neurologic assessment q15–30min during/after infusion; BP every 15 min (goal <180/105 during/24h after); hold antithrombotic x 24h after tPA; CT/MRI before tPA (rule out hemorrhage). NIHSS. Serial BP (hypertension management required — labetalol, nicardipine). Avoid Foley/NG/arterial lines for 30 min after infusion if possible.
ddi: Anticoagulants (additive bleeding risk — check INR/aPTT; stroke contraindications include INR >1.7, elevated aPTT, DOAC within 48 h, therapeutic LMWH within 24 h). Antiplatelet agents (increased ICH risk — prior aspirin use does not preclude tPA, but hold all antiplatelets/anticoagulants for 24 h post-tPA). Heparin (contraindicated concurrently in stroke). ACE inhibitors (↑ orolingual angioedema risk).
pearls: Time-sensitive: "Time is brain" (stroke window 4.5h or 3h, STEMI 12h). NINDS rt-PA Study (1995): improved stroke outcomes 30% with tPA (though ↑ hemorrhage risk). Contraindications: prior ICH, active bleeding, recent surgery, BP >185/110. Reperfusion arrhythmias common in STEMI (prepare for ACLS). ICH risk highest if age >80, weight <70 kg, on anticoagulants. PCI preferred over fibrinolysis if available (better outcomes, lower bleeding). Updated after the 2024 course: Tenecteplase gained FDA stroke approval Mar 2025.
trials: NINDS tPA stroke trial (NEJM 1995), ECASS III (4.5h window), NOR-TEST 2 (tenecteplase vs alteplase)
pk: t½ ~4–5 min (plasma clearance rapid). Bioavailability: IV only. Hepatic clearance. Fibrin-specific tPA; binds fibrin-bound plasminogen selectively.
highyield:
• Ischemic stroke: 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) within 4.5 h of symptom onset; give 10% as bolus, rest over 60 min
• STEMI: accelerated infusion (front-loaded) when PCI not available within 120 min
• Absolute contraindications for stroke: prior ICH, ischemic stroke within 3 months, severe head trauma, active bleeding, uncontrolled HTN >185/110
• Monitor for angioedema (1–5%) — hold ACEi before tPA or monitor closely
• BP must be <185/110 before and ≤180/105 during/after tPA infusion

name: Atorvastatin
moa: Reversible inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase (rate-limiting step in cholesterol synthesis); ↓ LDL-C 30-50%+; ↑ HDL-C; ↓ TG
indications: Primary prevention (age 40-75 with CVD risk factors, LDL ≥70, or ASCVD 10yr >7.5%); secondary prevention (CVD, ACS, post-MI, post-stent); stroke prevention; familial hypercholesterolemia
dosing: PO: 10-20 mg daily (moderate intensity, ↓ LDL 30-49%), or 40-80 mg daily (high-intensity, ↓ LDL ≥50%); titrate by lipid response q4-12 weeks; max 80 mg daily
renal: No dose adjustment; severe renal disease: minimal metabolites
hepatic: Contraindicated in acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis (current labeling; replaced the older "active liver disease/unexplained persistent transaminase elevation" contraindication); baseline LFTs; chronic liver disease/heavy alcohol use: caution
ades: Myalgia/muscle pain (5-10%); statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS, myopathy, rhabdomyolysis rare <0.1%); liver injury (persistent transaminase elevation >3× ULN ~0.7%; clinically significant hepatotoxicity rare); new-onset diabetes (slight risk); cognitive effects (rare, reversible)
monitoring: Baseline lipid panel (TC, LDL, HDL, TG), LFTs, CK (if symptomatic); repeat lipids q4-12 weeks to goal; LFTs at baseline, repeat only if clinically indicated (routine periodic LFTs not recommended); muscle symptoms/pain assessment; glucose (diabetes risk screening)
ddi: CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin/itraconazole ↑ exposure ~3-4.5× — max 20 mg/day; tipranavir/ritonavir ~9× — avoid; erythromycin, other boosted protease inhibitors: dose limits; risk myopathy); fibrates (gemfibrozil: ↑ myopathy risk significantly); niacin (↑ myopathy); cyclosporine (↑ myopathy); warfarin (monitor INR)
pearls: High-intensity statin (40-80 mg daily). ASCOT-LLA, CARDS, SPARCL, TNT, PROVE-IT TIMI 22 (80 mg vs pravastatin): ↓ CV events (WOSCOPS = pravastatin; JUPITER/HOPE-3 = rosuvastatin). LDL goal varies (typically <70 mg/dL post-ACS, <100 mg/dL primary prevention). Statin intolerance: switch to lower-dose, every-other-day, or alternative statin (pravastatin less CYP3A4). SAMS: not all muscle pain is statin-related (context important). Reduce dose if combining with CYP3A4 inhibitors.
trials: WOSCOPS, ASCOT, JUPITER, HOPE-3
pk: t½ ~14 h (active metabolites ~20–30 h). Bioavailability ~14% (first-pass). Protein binding ≥98%. Metabolized by CYP3A4. Excretion: biliary/fecal ~98%.
highyield: • Strong/moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, diltiazem, verapamil) ↑ atorvastatin → myopathy risk; amlodipine raises exposure only mildly (no dose limit; co-formulated as Caduet)

name: Rosuvastatin
moa: Potent reversible HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor; ↓ LDL-C 40-55%+ (most potent statin); ↑ HDL-C; ↓ TG; minimal hepatic metabolism
indications: Primary/secondary ASCVD prevention (high-intensity LDL lowering); familial hypercholesterolemia; severe hypertriglyceridemia reduction
dosing: PO: 5-10 mg daily (moderate, ↓ LDL 30-49%), or 20-40 mg daily (high-intensity, ↓ LDL ≥50%); Asian ancestry: start 5 mg (increased statin exposure); max 40 mg daily
renal: Severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min/1.73 m2) not on hemodialysis: start 5 mg daily, max 10 mg daily; mild-moderate: no adjustment; hemodialysis: no specific label adjustment (monitor for myopathy)
hepatic: Contraindicated in acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis; chronic liver disease/heavy alcohol use: caution (exposure ↑ in Child-Pugh B)
ades: Myalgia/myopathy (↑ vs atorvastatin in some reports); new-onset diabetes (slight risk); transaminase elevation >3× ULN (~1%); rhabdomyolysis (rare; ↑ with 40 mg, Asian ancestry, renal impairment); myositis (very rare); dose-related proteinuria/hematuria (mainly 40 mg)
monitoring: Baseline lipid panel, LFTs, CK (baseline if symptoms); repeat lipids q4-12 weeks to goal; LFTs baseline (repeat if symptoms only); muscle symptoms assessment; glucose screening
ddi: Rosuvastatin is NOT a CYP3A4 substrate — interactions are transporter-mediated (OATP1B1/BCRP): cyclosporine (↑ AUC ~4-7×; limit rosuvastatin to 5 mg/day); gemfibrozil (↑ AUC ~2×; avoid, or limit to 10 mg/day); certain protease inhibitors e.g. atazanavir/ritonavir, lopinavir/ritonavir (↑ AUC; limit to 10 mg/day); warfarin (monitor INR). Pure CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) do NOT significantly raise rosuvastatin.
pearls: Most potent statin (highest LDL ↓ 40-55% standard dosing). Asian ancestry: ↑ statin exposure (start 5 mg). Minimal hepatic metabolism = fewer CYP interactions vs atorvastatin. JUPITER (2008): ↓ CV events even in low-baseline LDL. More myalgia reports vs atorvastatin (may be more potent effect). Avoid in patients on gemfibrozil/cyclosporine.
trials: JUPITER, STELLAR, LUNAR
pk: t½ ~19 h. Bioavailability ~20%. Protein binding ~88%. NOT significantly metabolized by CYP3A4 (minor CYP2C9). P-gp/OATP1B1 substrate. Excretion: fecal ~90%.
highyield:
• High-intensity statin: 20–40 mg/day; LDL lowering ~55–63% at 40 mg
• JUPITER trial: reduced CV events in patients with normal LDL but elevated hsCRP
• Fewer CYP3A4 interactions than atorvastatin — preferred with CYP3A4-heavy regimens
• Asian patients: start at 5 mg (higher plasma levels); max 20 mg if on certain drugs
• Dose reduce with certain HIV/transplant drugs (OATP1B1 inhibitors: cyclosporine → max 5 mg)

name: Evolocumab
class: PCSK9 Inhibitor (Monoclonal Antibody; IgG2 Fully Human)
moa: Monoclonal antibody binds PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9); prevents PCSK9-mediated LDL receptor degradation; ↑ LDL receptor recycling → ↓ LDL-C additional 50-60% on statin
indications: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (FHC); clinical ASCVD (post-MI, post-stent, stable CAD, stroke) requiring additional LDL lowering; homozygous FHC (PCSK9 BB); statin intolerance with LDL goal unmet
dosing: SC: for primary hyperlipidemia/HeFH/ASCVD — 140 mg Q2 weeks OR 420 mg once monthly (equivalent). For homozygous FH — 420 mg once monthly (or 420 mg Q2 weeks if on LDL apheresis); the 140 mg Q2wk regimen is not adequate for HoFH.
renal: No dose adjustment
hepatic: No specific adjustment
ades: Local injection site reactions (erythema, swelling, pain: 2-3%); muscle symptoms (PCSK9i myopathy rare, <1%); upper respiratory infections; fatigue; LDL-C <25 mg/dL (very low, long-term CV benefit unclear but no harm observed); anti-evolocumab antibodies (rare, may reduce efficacy)
monitoring: Baseline lipid panel (especially LDL-C); repeat lipids 4-12 weeks post-initiation to confirm LDL lowering; annual lipids; injection site assessment; muscle symptoms (baseline if SAMS history); cardiac event history
ddi: Minimal drug interactions (monoclonal antibody, no CYP metabolism); combine with statin ± ezetimibe for additive effect; additive benefits with other lipid-lowering agents
pearls: FOURIER (2017): ↓ CV events (MI/stroke/CV death) 15% with evolocumab + statin. Expensive (~$6,000/year list price after the 2018 cut from ~$14,000; before insurance). Can achieve LDL <30-50 mg/dL (very low, optimal in post-ACS). Inject SC Q2 or Q4 weeks (home-injectable). Monoclonal antibody = minimal drug interactions. Anti-drug binding antibodies are rare (~0.3%; none neutralizing; no effect on efficacy). CMS/insurance coverage typically requires statin failure/intolerance or FHC.
trials: FOURIER, DESCARTES, MENDEL
pk: t½ ~11–17 days. Bioavailability ~72% (SC injection). Protein binding: binds PCSK9 (endogenous target). Eliminated by proteolytic degradation (not renal/hepatic CYP).
highyield:
• Monoclonal antibody binding PCSK9 → prevents LDL-R degradation → ↑ LDL clearance
• FOURIER trial: 59% LDL reduction; 15% RRR in CV events on top of statin therapy
• FDA-approved: heterozygous/homozygous FH, ASCVD with inadequate statin response
• Injection every 2 weeks (140 mg) or monthly (420 mg) — subcutaneous
• Most common ADEs: injection site reactions, nasopharyngitis, flu-like symptoms

name: Ezetimibe
moa: Inhibits Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 (NPC1L1) protein in intestinal brush border; blocks cholesterol/phytosterol absorption in small intestine; ↓ LDL-C 15-20% monotherapy
indications: Mild-moderate hypercholesterolemia (adjunct to statin or monotherapy if statin intolerant); familial hypercholesterolemia; combined hyperlipidemia
dosing: PO: 10 mg daily (taken with or without food); combine with statin for additive effect (additional ~20-25% LDL ↓); can combine with PCSK9i
renal: No dose adjustment; severe renal impairment: minimal data (likely safe)
hepatic: Moderate-severe cirrhosis: avoid (↑ ezetimibe levels)
ades: Myalgia/myopathy (when combined with statin); GI upset; headache; arthralgia; cholecystitis (rare, association uncertain); angioedema (rare)
monitoring: Baseline lipid panel; repeat lipids 4-12 weeks; LFTs if combined with statin; muscle symptoms if statin + ezetimibe
ddi: Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol: ↓ ezetimibe absorption by ~55%; give ezetimibe ≥2 h before or ≥4 h after the sequestrant); fibrates (monitor myopathy risk); statins (additive effect, monitor SAMS); cyclosporine (↑ ezetimibe levels)
pearls: IMPROVE-IT (2015): ezetimibe + simvastatin ↓ CV events vs simvastatin alone (LDL 54 vs 70 mg/dL; ~2% absolute/6.4% relative ↓ in CV events = modest additional CV benefit). Not as potent as PCSK9i but cheaper. Additive with statin (additional ~20-25% LDL ↓). GI side effects minimal. No direct CV mortality reduction trials. Useful adjunct for statin-intolerant patients or maximizing LDL ↓.
trials: IMPROVE-IT, SANDS
pk: t½ ~22 h. Bioavailability ~35–65%. Protein binding ezetimibe ~99%, ezetimibe-glucuronide ~88%. Metabolized by glucuronidation (not CYP). Excretion: fecal ~78%, renal ~11%.
highyield: • Efficacy does not require a gallbladder — acts at the intestinal brush border (NPC1L1); separate dosing from bile-acid sequestrants (give ≥2 h before or ≥4 h after) as they reduce ezetimibe absorption ~55%

name: Hydralazine/Isosorbide Dinitrate
moa: Hydralazine: arteriolar vasodilator (↓ afterload, reflex tachycardia); Isosorbide dinitrate: nitrate (venodilator, ↓ preload); combined: ↑ nitric oxide bioavailability, ↓ sympathetic tone
indications: HFrEF in self-identified Black patients (FDA-approved race-specific indication, A-HeFT trial; NYHA III-IV, added to ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA); HFrEF patients who cannot take ACEi/ARB/ARNI (intolerance, renal insufficiency, hyperkalemia)
dosing: BiDil (37.5 mg hydralazine/20 mg ISDN per tablet): 1 tablet PO TID, titrate (over 3-5 days as tolerated) to max 2 tablets TID (75 mg/40 mg TID); may reduce to ½ tablet TID if side effects. Separate components: hydralazine 25-50 mg TID-QID + ISDN 20-30 mg TID-QID, titrate to target hydralazine up to 300 mg/day + ISDN 120 mg/day (40 mg TID); TID dosing as in A-HeFT (no formal nitrate-free interval in HF regimens)
renal: CrCl 10-50: reduce hydralazine dose; CrCl <10: caution, nitrate accumulation risk
hepatic: Cirrhosis: caution (nitrates metabolized hepatically)
ades: Headache (most common, ~50%), dizziness, hypotension, reflex tachycardia; drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, dose- and slow-acetylator-related); peripheral neuropathy (pyridoxine-responsive)
monitoring: Baseline ECG, vital signs; periodic HR/BP (reflex tachycardia risk); ANA (hydralazine lupus screen if symptoms); symptoms of decompensation
ddi: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil: profound hypotension, CONTRAINDICATED); other nitrates (↑ nitrate effect, spacing required); NSAIDs (↓ vasodilator effect); sympathomimetics (counteract vasodilation)
pearls: A-HeFT (2005): Black HF patients on hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate + standard HF therapy (ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, diuretic) showed ↓ mortality 43% vs placebo. Race-specific indication (FDA approval). Reflex tachycardia → add beta-blocker. Nitrate tolerance: hydralazine may attenuate it; HF regimens use TID dosing without a formal nitrate-free interval. Used when ACEi/ARB contraindicated or intolerant. BiDil formulation (fixed-dose) = compliance advantage.
trials: A-HeFT
pk: Hydralazine: t½ ~1–4 h; bioavailability varies (acetylation polymorphism — fast vs slow acetylators). ISDN: t½ ~1–4 h; bioavailability ~20–25%. Both hepatically metabolized.
highyield:
• A-HeFT trial: 43% mortality reduction in self-identified Black patients with HFrEF on top of standard therapy
• BiDil is fixed-dose combination — labeled specifically for Black patients (racial subgroup evidence)
• Lupus-like syndrome with hydralazine in slow acetylators (higher doses, >200 mg/day)
• Hydralazine: direct arterial vasodilator (↓ afterload); ISDN: venodilator (↓ preload)
• Alternative to ACEi/ARB when both are truly intolerable (renal, angioedema)

name: Mavacamten
moa: Direct allosteric inhibition of cardiac myosin motor protein; reduces cardiac myosin-actin force generation; improves LV obstruction and diastolic function in HCM
indications: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) with left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction; symptomatic HCM to reduce outflow obstruction and improve exercise capacity (EXPLORER-HCM)
dosing: Start 5 mg once daily (only if LVEF ≥55%); titrate within the 2.5–15 mg once-daily range based on Valsalva LVOT gradient and LVEF (echo at weeks 4 and 8; no up-titration before week 12); maximum recommended dose is 15 mg once daily (available strengths 2.5, 5, 10, 15 mg). Weak CYP2C19 or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor started: reduce by one dose level.
renal: No dose adjustment; severe renal disease: limited data
hepatic: Mild-moderate (Child-Pugh A/B): no dose adjustment (exposure ↑ up to ~220%; rely on echo-guided titration); severe (Child-Pugh C): not studied
ades: HF exacerbation/reduced EF (↓ contractility, ↑ HFrEF risk if EF already reduced); hypotension; dizziness; fatigue; bradycardia; syncope (from reduced contractility); back pain
monitoring: Echocardiogram at baseline (do not initiate if LVEF <55%), then at Weeks 4, 8, and 12 during titration, then every 12 weeks; per the April 2025 label update, stable maintenance patients (Week ≥12, LVEF ≥55%, Valsalva LVOT gradient <30 mmHg) may extend echo monitoring to every 6 months. Interrupt therapy if LVEF <50% at any visit. Updated after the 2024 course: April 2025 label reduced echo frequency.
ddi: CYP2C19 (major) and CYP3A4 substrate — 2024 label CONTRAINDICATES moderate-to-strong CYP2C19 inhibitors (e.g., fluconazole, fluvoxamine, ticlopidine) and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir), and moderate-to-strong CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort); weak CYP2C19/moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors: reduce dose one level. Negative inotropes (beta-blockers, CCBs, disopyramide: additive effect, use with caution); progestin-containing hormonal contraceptives (↓ efficacy; use alternative contraception); anticoagulants if AFib develops (HCM+AFib ↑ stroke risk). Updated after the 2024 course: the April 2025 label allows moderate CYP2C19 inhibitors and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors with dose adjustment (FDA/BMS, 2025).
pearls: Not a contraindication but a boxed-warning/dosing restriction: do not initiate if LVEF <55%; during treatment maintain LVEF ≥50% (do not up-titrate if LVEF <50%); interrupt therapy if LVEF <50% at any visit.
trials: EXPLORER-HCM, VALOR-HCM
pk: t½ ~6–9 days in CYP2C19 normal metabolizers (~23 days in poor metabolizers). Bioavailability ≥85%. Protein binding 97–98%. Metabolized primarily by CYP2C19 (74%), CYP3A4 (18%), CYP2C9 (8%). Excretion: renal ~85%, fecal ~7% (mostly metabolites).
bbw: HEART FAILURE RISK: Can cause heart failure due to systolic dysfunction. Echo LVEF required before and during treatment; initiation not recommended if LVEF <55%; interrupt if LVEF <50% or worsening clinical status. Concomitant use with certain CYP450 inhibitors or discontinuation of certain inducers can increase HF risk: contraindicated with moderate-to-strong CYP2C19 inhibitors or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and with moderate-to-strong CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 inducers (2024 label). Available only through REMS program (Camzyos REMS). Updated after the 2024 course: the April 2025 label moved moderate CYP2C19 inhibitors and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors from contraindications to dose-adjusted interactions (FDA/BMS, 2025).
highyield: 2024 label: contraindicated with moderate-to-strong CYP2C19 inhibitors, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and moderate-to-strong CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 inducers (↑ exposure → HF, or loss of effect). Updated after the 2024 course: the April 2025 label update made moderate CYP2C19 inhibitors and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors manageable interactions requiring dose adjustment/monitoring; strong CYP2C19 inhibitors and moderate-to-strong CYP2C19/CYP3A4 inducers remain contraindicated (FDA/BMS, Apr 2025). Updated after the 2024 course: April 2025 label reclassified the CYP interactions.

name: Vancomycin
moa: Inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, blocking transglycosylation/transpeptidation. Bactericidal against gram-positives (time-independent; AUC/MIC-driven).
indications: MRSA infections (bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia, skin/soft tissue, osteomyelitis); C. diff colitis (PO only); VRE (last resort); coagulase-negative Staph.
dosing: IV: 15–20 mg/kg q8–12h (based on AUC/MIC target 400–600 mg·h/L per ASHP/IDSA 2020 guidelines). PO: 125 mg QID x 10d (C.diff). Loading dose 25–30 mg/kg if critically ill. Infuse over ≥60 min (1g); max rate 10 mg/min to prevent Red Man Syndrome.
renal: Primarily renally eliminated; CrCl <50 requires interval extension. HD: redose post-dialysis (500 mg–1g depending on session).
hepatic: No dose adjustment needed.
ades: Nephrotoxicity (esp. with concomitant piperacillin-tazobactam or aminoglycosides), ototoxicity (high troughs/prolonged therapy), Red Man Syndrome (rate-related, not true allergy — flushing/pruritus of face/neck), thrombophlebitis, DRESS.
monitoring: AUC/MIC monitoring (Bayesian pharmacokinetic software preferred); obtain 2 levels (pre and post 4th dose or per PK program). Older trough-based: 15–20 mg/L (MRSA bacteremia/endocarditis). SCr, CBC (neutropenia), LFTs. Audiometry if prolonged.
ddi: Synergistic nephrotoxicity: aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, loop diuretics, contrast. Additive nephrotoxicity with piperacillin-tazobactam (controversial but monitor closely).
pearls: AUC/MIC-guided dosing is now standard of care (2020 consensus guidelines). Red Man Syndrome prevented by slowing infusion or pre-medicating with diphenhydramine. Dose by actual body weight, including in obesity (loading 20–25 mg/kg actual BW, max 3,000 mg; maintenance AUC-guided) — adjusted body weight is not recommended. Not effective for gram-negatives. Oral vancomycin NOT absorbed systemically (used only for GI indications).
trials: ASHP/IDSA/SIDP Vancomycin Consensus 2020, Rybak et al. AJHP 2020
pk: t½ ~4–8 h (renally dependent). Bioavailability: IV only (oral not absorbed — used for C. diff). Protein binding 55%. Not metabolized. Excretion: renal 80–90% unchanged (GFR-dependent).
bbw: No boxed warning for standard vancomycin; nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are Warnings & Precautions. (A boxed warning for fetal malformations applies ONLY to certain premixed ready-to-use IV formulations containing PEG 400 and NADA excipients, if used in the first/second trimester.)
highyield:
• AUC/MIC-guided dosing preferred over trough-only: target AUC₂₄ 400–600 mg·h/L
• Red man syndrome (vancomycin flushing syndrome): not allergy — slow infusion rate (≥60 min), premedicate with antihistamine
• Narrow therapeutic index: nephrotoxicity (especially with piperacillin-tazobactam, aminoglycosides)
• MRSA coverage requires IV (oral = C. diff only)
• Loading dose 25–30 mg/kg IV for serious/bacteremic infections

name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam
moa: Piperacillin inhibits cell wall synthesis (binds PBPs). Tazobactam is a beta-lactamase inhibitor (irreversible suicide inhibitor of class A/C enzymes). Time-dependent killing; optimize by extended infusion.
indications: Intra-abdominal infections, nosocomial pneumonia (HAP/VAP), complicated UTI, skin/soft tissue, febrile neutropenia, Pseudomonas coverage.
dosing: 3.375 g IV q6h (standard); 4.5 g IV q6h; Extended infusion: 3.375 g infused over 4h q8h (preferred for Pseudomonas MIC 16–32 mcg/mL — maximizes % time above MIC). Renal dosing required.
renal: CrCl 20–40: 2.25 g q6h. CrCl <20: 2.25 g q8h. ESRD/HD: 2.25 g q12h + 0.75 g after HD sessions. Nosocomial pneumonia (usual 4.5 g q6h): CrCl 20–40: 3.375 g q6h; CrCl <20: 2.25 g q6h; HD: 2.25 g q8h + 0.75 g after each HD session.
hepatic: No adjustment unless concurrent severe renal impairment.
ades: GI upset, diarrhea, electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia; high sodium load — 2.84 mEq Na/g piperacillin — caution in sodium-restricted/HF patients), hepatotoxicity (rare), thrombocytopenia, seizures (high doses), nephrotoxicity (debated synergy with vancomycin).
monitoring: SCr/BUN, CBC, electrolytes. Culture-directed therapy when possible. Drug fever — suspect if no other cause.
ddi: Vancomycin (AKI risk debate), methotrexate (decreased clearance), anticoagulants (hypoprothrombinemia risk), aminoglycosides (inactivation if mixed in same IV bag — separate administration).
pearls: Extended infusion improves PK/PD target attainment for MIC-creeping organisms (Pseudomonas). Does NOT cover MRSA, VRE, Stenotrophomonas, or Acinetobacter reliably. Penicillin allergy — assess cross-reactivity risk; aztreonam may substitute for gram-negative coverage. MERINO trial: pip-tazo inferior to meropenem for ESBL bacteremia (carbapenem preferred for ESBL).
trials: MERINO trial (Harris et al. JAMA 2018), Lodise extended infusion studies
pk: t½ piperacillin/tazobactam ~1 h. Bioavailability: IV only. Protein binding ~30%. Minimal hepatic metabolism. Excretion: renal ~68% (piperacillin), ~80% (tazobactam) unchanged.
highyield: Vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam: observational/meta-analytic data show ↑ AKI signal vs vancomycin alone — consider monitoring or alternative anti-pseudomonal. Note: signal may be confounded (e.g., creatinine assay interference/pseudo-nephrotoxicity); ACORN RCT (cefepime vs pip-tazo, JAMA 2023) found no AKI difference. (No AKIKI reference — AKIKI = RRT initiation-timing trial.)

name: Meropenem
moa: Broad-spectrum beta-lactam; binds PBPs 2 and 3, inhibiting cell wall synthesis. Stable to most beta-lactamases including ESBLs and AmpC. Time-dependent killing.
indications: Severe gram-negative infections (ESBL, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter); polymicrobial intra-abdominal; meningitis; febrile neutropenia; HAP/VAP. Drug of choice for ESBL-producing organisms (MERINO trial).
dosing: 1 g IV q8h (standard); 2 g IV q8h (Pseudomonas, CNS infections). Extended infusion: 2 g over 3h q8h for highly resistant organisms. Meningitis: 2 g q8h.
renal: CrCl 26–50: 1 g q12h. CrCl 10–25: 0.5 g q12h. CrCl <10: 0.5 g q24h. HD: dose after dialysis.
hepatic: No adjustment needed.
ades: GI (N/V/D), seizures (lower seizure risk than imipenem — preferred for CNS), hypersensitivity (cross-reactivity ~1% with penicillin allergy), hepatotoxicity (transient LFT elevation), thrombocytopenia.
monitoring: Culture/susceptibility, SCr, CBC. Watch for Clostridioides difficile with prolonged use. Seizure threshold monitoring.
ddi: Valproic acid — dramatic reduction in valproate levels (do not use together; use alternative anticonvulsant or antibiotic). Probenecid (increases levels).
pearls: Preferred carbapenem for CNS infections (less epileptogenic than imipenem). MERINO trial (ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli/Klebsiella bacteremia): piperacillin-tazobactam failed to show noninferiority to meropenem (30-day mortality 12.3% vs 3.7%) — carbapenem preferred for ESBL bacteremia (AmpC data from MERINO-2 inconclusive). Carbapenem-resistant organisms (CRE): novel beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors as monotherapy preferred (KPC: meropenem-vaborbactam, ceftazidime-avibactam, imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam; MBL: ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam or cefiderocol); routine combination therapy not recommended (IDSA AMR guidance 2024). Meropenem-vaborbactam (Vabomere) covers KPC-producing CRE.
trials: MERINO (JAMA 2018), CARBAVAR trial, TANGO II (meropenem-vaborbactam)
pk: t½ ~1 h. Bioavailability: IV only. Protein binding ~2%. Minimal hepatic metabolism (hydrolysis). Excretion: renal ~70% unchanged.
highyield: Lower seizure risk (less epileptogenic) than imipenem-cilastatin — preferred carbapenem for CNS infections.

name: Daptomycin
