ades: Hypokalemia (potassium wasting — monitor K+, supplement), hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia (vs. thiazides which cause hypercalcemia), metabolic alkalosis (contraction alkalosis), ototoxicity (high doses IV, esp. with aminoglycosides), volume depletion/prerenal azotemia, gout (uricosuria decreased → hyperuricemia), photosensitivity. Sulfonamide-based — cross-reactivity consideration.
monitoring: BMP (Na+, K+, Mg2+, BUN/Cr) daily when IV or dose changes; urine output; daily weight; signs of volume depletion (orthostasis, dry mucous membranes). Spot urine Na+ can gauge adequacy of response.
ddi: Aminoglycosides/cisplatin (additive ototoxicity), NSAIDs (decreased diuretic effect + AKI risk), probenecid (blocks tubular secretion → decreased effect), lithium (increased toxicity — decreased clearance), digoxin (hypokalemia increases toxicity risk), corticosteroids (additive hypokalemia).
pearls: Loop diuretics work in loop of Henle — effective even when GFR is low (unlike thiazides, which need GFR >30). DOSE trial: continuous infusion vs. intermittent bolus — no significant difference in outcomes; intermittent bolus preferred for most. Furosemide resistance: consider adding thiazide (metolazone 2.5–5 mg 30 min before furosemide) for synergistic sequential nephron blockade. Acoustic nerve monitoring if prolonged high-dose IV use.
trials: DOSE trial (Felker NEJM 2011 — high vs. low dose, bolus vs. continuous), CARRESS-HF
pk: t½ ~2 h. Bioavailability 60–70% (oral, variable; IV 100%). Protein binding ~91–99%. Minimal hepatic metabolism. Excretion: renal ~66% unchanged.
bbw: Furosemide is a potent diuretic which, if given in excessive amounts, can lead to a profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion. Therefore, careful medical supervision is required and dose and dose schedule must be adjusted to the individual patient's needs. (Circulatory collapse/thrombosis/embolism in the elderly and ototoxicity with rapid IV use, renal impairment, or aminoglycosides are in Warnings — not part of the boxed text.)
highyield: Ceiling effect: dose-response reaches plateau (max effective dose); DOSE trial found NO significant difference between continuous infusion and intermittent bolus in ADHF (intermittent bolus is acceptable first-line)

name: Sodium Bicarbonate
moa: Bicarbonate (HCO3−) is the body's primary buffer: HCO3− + H+ → H2CO3 → H2O + CO2. IV administration raises serum pH. Also shifts K+ intracellularly (useful for acute hyperkalemia), alkalinizes urine (enhances excretion of weak acids), and replaces renal bicarbonate losses in RTA/CKD.
indications: Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1, bicarbonate <10 mEq/L — controversial); cardiac arrest (prolonged, with adequate ventilation); hyperkalemia (temporizing measure — shifts K+ intracellularly); TCA overdose (alkalinization for cardiac toxicity); urinary alkalinization (rhabdomyolysis protection, uric acid stones, salicylate overdose); RTA type I/II; CKD-associated metabolic acidosis (oral).
dosing: Cardiac arrest/severe acidosis: 1 mEq/kg IV bolus. Metabolic acidosis: calculated deficit = (24 - current HCO3) × 0.5 × weight (kg); give 50% over 4–6h. Hyperkalemia: 50 mEq IV over 5 min (temporizing). Oral CKD: 650 mg TID–QID titrated to HCO3 target 22–26 mEq/L.
renal: Monitor fluid balance (hyperosmolarity + volume load). Titrate to serum HCO3 levels. In CKD, small RCTs (de Brito-Ashurst 2009; UBI 2019) suggested slower CKD progression, but the larger BiCARB trial (2020) showed no benefit; KDIGO 2024 suggests treating when serum HCO3 <18 mmol/L and not exceeding the upper limit of normal.
hepatic: No specific adjustment; avoid in patients with sodium-sensitive conditions (cirrhosis with ascites).
ades: Metabolic alkalosis (overshoot), hypernatremia (high sodium load — 50 mEq NaHCO3 = 50 mEq Na+), volume overload, hypocalcemia (alkalosis shifts Ca2+ to albumin-bound state → ionized Ca2+ drops → tetany, seizures), hypokalemia, paradoxical CSF acidosis (CO2 crosses BBB faster than HCO3), tissue necrosis if extravasation.
monitoring: Arterial blood gas (pH, pCO2, HCO3), serum electrolytes (Na+, K+, Ca2+), ionized calcium (especially if tetany), osmolality, fluid status.
ddi: Quinolones, tetracyclines, iron supplements (decreased absorption with oral NaHCO3 — separate by 2h). Lithium (alkalinization increases renal excretion — may decrease lithium levels). Aspirin (alkalinization increases salicylate excretion — use intentionally in overdose). Amphetamines (decreased excretion with alkaline urine — retain in body).
pearls: Controversial in cardiac arrest: routine use NOT recommended (AHA guidelines) — CO2 generated can worsen intracellular acidosis and impair hemodynamics; use after prolonged arrest or specific indications (TCA toxicity, hyperkalemia). In TCA overdose: target serum pH 7.45–7.55 (alkalemia narrows Na+ channel blockade — monitor QRS width). Urinary alkalinization: maintain urine pH >6.5 for rhabdomyolysis protection or uric acid nephrolithiasis. Monitor ionized calcium carefully — alkalosis drops ionized Ca2+.
trials: BICAR-ICU trial (Jaber LANCET 2018 — bicarbonate in severe metabolic acidosis in ICU)
pk: Endogenous buffer. IV infusion or oral tablets. Distributes to extracellular fluid. Rapidly dissociates to Na⁺ and HCO₃⁻. Renal regulation of bicarbonate.
highyield:
• Indications: metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1), hyperkalemia (temporizing), TCA overdose (wide QRS), urinary alkalinization
• Overshoot alkalosis risk — titrate carefully; goal HCO₃⁻ 15–20 mEq/L in acute IV therapy (not full correction)
• Hypokalemia and hypocalcemia worsen with rapid administration (K⁺ shifts into cells; ionized Ca²⁺ binds albumin)
• Incompatible with calcium solutions (precipitates calcium carbonate)
• Urine alkalinization increases excretion of salicylates, phenobarbital, methotrexate

name: Sevelamer
moa: Polymer containing multiple amine groups that protonates in GI tract → positively charged → binds dietary phosphate anions in intestinal lumen via ion exchange and hydrogen bonding → prevents phosphate absorption → reduces serum phosphate. Also binds bile acids (LDL-lowering effect) and uric acid. NOT absorbed systemically.
indications: Hyperphosphatemia in CKD stages 3–5, dialysis-dependent patients. Preferred over calcium-based binders when serum Ca2+ is elevated or when cardiovascular calcification risk is a concern.
dosing: Initial (Renvela, not on a binder): 800 mg TID with meals if serum phosphorus >5.5 to <7.5 mg/dL; 1600 mg TID with meals if ≥7.5 mg/dL. Titrate by 800 mg per meal q2 weeks to target phosphorus <5.5 mg/dL. Must be taken WITH meals.
renal: Used specifically in CKD/ESRD. No systemic absorption → no renal dose adjustment.
hepatic: No dose adjustment needed (not absorbed).
ades: GI (nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, dyspepsia — most common; causes poor adherence), dysphagia (large tablets — use powder form for swallowing difficulty), pill burden (large number of tablets/day), metabolic acidosis (Renagel HCl version delivers chloride load — use Renvela carbonate to avoid), bowel obstruction/perforation (rare, serious).
monitoring: Serum phosphorus (target CKD-MBD guidelines: dialysis patients <5.5 mg/dL), calcium, PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism monitoring), pill burden assessment, lipid panel (sevelamer lowers LDL — monitor), CBC (anemia of CKD).
ddi: Multiple medications: sevelamer can bind certain drugs (ciprofloxacin ~50% ↓, mycophenolate, levothyroxine, cyclosporine/tacrolimus — no effect on warfarin, digoxin, metoprolol, enalapril, iron) → decreased absorption. Administer these drugs at least 1h before or 3h after sevelamer. Reduced bile acid absorption may affect fat-soluble vitamin absorption (A, D, E, K).
pearls: DCOR trial: sevelamer vs. calcium-based binders — sevelamer does NOT reduce mortality but associated with fewer hypercalcemic episodes and possibly less vascular calcification progression. Calcium carbonate is cheaper and effective first-line if Ca2+ is normal. Pill burden is a major adherence barrier (often 9–12 tablets/day with meals). Renvela (carbonate) preferred over Renagel (HCl) to avoid exacerbating metabolic acidosis in CKD patients.
trials: DCOR trial (Suki NEJM 2007), LANDMARK trial, INDEPENDENT trial
pk: NOT absorbed systemically — acts locally in GI tract. Binds phosphate in intestinal lumen → fecal excretion. No systemic PK/PD of note.
highyield:
• Non-calcium phosphate binder — preferred in CKD patients with hypercalcemia or vascular calcification
• Sevelamer HCl (Renagel) can worsen metabolic acidosis; sevelamer carbonate (Renvela) is bicarbonate-buffered (preferred)
• Reduces LDL cholesterol as secondary benefit (bile acid binding)
• Take with meals — must be taken with food; never crush tablets (risk of expansion)
• Give levothyroxine, fluoroquinolones, and other interacting drugs ≥1 h before or 3 h after sevelamer (binds drugs)

name: Pantoprazole
moa: Irreversibly inhibits H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) on gastric parietal cell secretory canaliculus → >90% reduction of acid secretion. Prodrug: acid-activated in secretory canaliculus → sulfenamide derivative → covalent binding to cysteines on proton pump. New acid secretion requires synthesis of new proton pump proteins (48–72h for full resynthesis after stopping PPI).
indications: GERD/erosive esophagitis (first-line); peptic ulcer disease (treatment + H. pylori eradication triple/quad therapy); stress ulcer prophylaxis (SUP) in mechanically ventilated ICU patients, coagulopathic, or major head/burn trauma; upper GI bleed (IV — high-dose infusion post-endoscopy); NSAID gastropathy prevention; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
dosing: GERD: 40 mg PO/IV daily. Erosive esophagitis: 40 mg PO once daily for up to 8 weeks (may repeat 8-week course). PUD (H. pylori): 40 mg BID x 10–14d + antibiotics. Upper GI bleed: 80 mg IV bolus then 8 mg/h continuous x 72h post-hemostasis. SUP ICU: 40 mg IV/PO daily.
renal: No dose adjustment needed. Minimal renal elimination (primarily hepatic metabolism).
hepatic: No dose adjustment needed (label); doses >40 mg/day not studied in hepatic impairment (AUC ↑5–7-fold, similar to CYP2C19 poor metabolizers). CYP2C19 metabolism reduced in poor metabolizers — higher AUC.
ades: Generally well-tolerated. Long-term risks: hypomagnesemia (>1 year — monitor Mg2+ annually), C. difficile risk (↑gastric pH promotes C. diff germination), pneumonia risk (aspiration with reduced acid barrier), bone fractures/osteoporosis (reduced Ca2+ absorption), B12 deficiency (intrinsic factor needs acid for B12 absorption), CKD association (observational — not clearly causal), SIADH (rare), interstitial nephritis.
monitoring: Serum magnesium annually with long-term use; H. pylori confirmation of eradication (UBT or stool antigen 4 weeks post-treatment); reassess SUP indication regularly (de-escalate when ICU risk factors resolve — prevent "PPI creep"); B12 levels with prolonged use in elderly.
ddi: Clopidogrel (CYP2C19 inhibition — reduced clopidogrel activation → decreased antiplatelet effect; pantoprazole has weaker interaction than omeprazole). Methotrexate (high-dose — reduced renal clearance). Rilpivirine-containing products (require acid for absorption — contraindicated with PPIs); atazanavir, nelfinavir (decreased exposure — see their labels; generally avoid). Mycophenolate (reduced absorption). Iron, ketoconazole (reduced absorption in alkaline environment).
pearls: PEPTIC trial (2020): PPI vs. H2RA stress ulcer prophylaxis in ventilated ICU patients — no difference in hospital mortality; slightly less clinically important GI bleeding with PPI. REVISE (2024): pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily vs placebo in ventilated patients ↓ clinically important upper GI bleeding without mortality difference. SUP de-escalation critical: only appropriate for high-risk ICU patients (mechanical ventilation >48h, coagulopathy, major burns/head trauma — ACCP/SCCM criteria). Most "PPI-prescribed" patients in hospital do NOT have a valid indication. Pantoprazole preferred over omeprazole in clopidogrel patients (weaker CYP2C19 inhibition). Take 30–60 min before meals for optimal efficacy (need active proton pumps). Long-term PPI: lowest effective dose, reassess annually.
trials: PEPTIC trial (NEJM 2020 — IV vs. oral PPI), SUP-ICU trial, TRITON-TIMI 38 (PPI + clopidogrel)
pk: t½ ~1–2 h. Bioavailability ~77% (oral). Protein binding ~98%. Metabolized by CYP2C19 (major), CYP3A4 (minor). Excretion: renal ~71% (metabolites).
highyield:
• PPI — irreversible H⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibitor; CYP2C19 genotype affects efficacy
• Hypomagnesemia with long-term use (>1 year) — check Mg²⁺ periodically
• Clopidogrel interaction: PPIs (especially omeprazole > pantoprazole) reduce active metabolite via CYP2C19
• C. difficile and community-acquired pneumonia risk with prolonged PPI therapy
• In ICU stress ulcer prophylaxis: PPIs superior to H2RAs for high-risk patients (mechanically ventilated, coagulopathy)

name: Rifaximin
moa: Inhibits bacterial RNA synthesis by binding beta-subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase → broad-spectrum antimicrobial effect concentrated in GI tract (>99.6% remains in gut lumen — <0.4% systemic absorption). Reduces ammonia-producing bacteria in gut → lowers serum ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy. Also modulates gut microbiome.
indications: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) — prevention of recurrence (FDA-approved with lactulose); traveler's diarrhea (non-invasive E. coli strains); IBS-D (irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea — 2-week course); small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO — off-label).
dosing: HE prophylaxis: 550 mg PO BID (with or without lactulose). Traveler's diarrhea: 200 mg TID x 3 days. IBS-D: 550 mg TID x 14 days (can retreat for recurrence).
renal: No dose adjustment (not systemically absorbed, excreted unchanged in feces).
hepatic: Cirrhotic patients: markedly increased systemic exposure (~10-, 14-, 21-fold in Child-Pugh A, B, C vs healthy, due to reduced metabolism/portosystemic shunting) — still low in absolute terms; no dose adjustment, but use with caution in Child-Pugh C (trials limited to MELD <25).
ades: Generally excellent tolerability (minimal systemic effects due to non-absorption). GI: nausea, abdominal pain, bloating, constipation (less than antibiotics). Peripheral edema (most common in HE trial, ~15%), dizziness, fatigue, ascites, anemia, pruritus. C. difficile risk is LOW (maintains normal gut flora better than systemic antibiotics). Hepatotoxicity (very rare).
monitoring: Mental status/HE grade (for HE prevention), liver function tests, serum ammonia (clinical correlation — ammonia level doesn't always predict HE severity), number of HE episodes per year, INR/albumin (liver function markers).
ddi: P-glycoprotein substrate but negligible interactions due to non-absorption. Warfarin (some reports of increased INR — monitor). P-gp inhibitors such as cyclosporine markedly increase rifaximin exposure (Cmax ~83-fold, AUC ~124-fold) — use caution, especially with hepatic impairment.
pearls: RFHE trial: rifaximin 550 mg BID reduced HE recurrence vs. placebo (22% vs 46% breakthrough HE over 6 months; NNT ≈ 4.2, reported as 4) and reduced hospitalizations. Adding rifaximin to lactulose is more effective than lactulose alone (91% of RFHE patients were on lactulose). Cost is significant ($1,500+/month) — access and adherence barriers. Unlike systemic antibiotics, rifaximin preserves gut microbiome diversity. For IBS-D: non-antibiotic mechanism proposed (microbiome modulation) — "gut-selective" antibiotic. SIBO: off-label but widely used (1200–1600 mg/day x 10–14 days).
trials: RFHE trial (Bass NEJM 2010 — rifaximin HE prevention), ILLUMINATE trial (IBS-D)
pk: t½ ~6 h. Bioavailability <0.4% (poorly absorbed — acts locally in GI). Protein binding ~68% (in plasma if absorbed). Metabolized minimally; primarily excreted fecally intact.
highyield:
• Minimally absorbed antibiotic — gut-selective; not for systemic infections
• FDA-approved: hepatic encephalopathy (HE) secondary prophylaxis (with or without lactulose), travelers' diarrhea, IBS-D
• RFHE trial: reduced HE recurrence by 58% vs placebo on top of lactulose
• Few drug interactions (poor absorption), but P-gp inhibitors (cyclosporine) greatly ↑ systemic exposure; minimal systemic side effects
• Rifaximin + lactulose combination more effective than lactulose alone for HE

name: Lactulose
moa: Non-absorbed synthetic disaccharide (galactose + fructose). Colonic bacteria ferment lactulose → lactic acid, acetic acid, formic acid → acidifies colonic contents (pH 5–5.5) → traps NH3 as NH4+ (ionized, non-absorbable) → reduces ammonia absorption. Osmotic effect draws water into colon → laxative effect (target 2–3 soft stools/day). Reduces blood ammonia.
indications: Hepatic encephalopathy — acute treatment and prophylaxis (standard first-line agent); constipation (occasional use); portal-systemic encephalopathy.
dosing: Acute HE: 20–30 g (30–45 mL; 10 g/15 mL) PO/NGT q1–2h until bowel movement; then 3–4x/day to target 2–3 soft stools/day. Maintenance: 20–30 g TID–QID (adjust to bowel habits). Rectal enema (if unable to take PO): 300 mL in 700 mL water, retained 30–60 min q4–6h. AVOID over-laxation (→ dehydration, electrolyte disturbances worsens HE).
renal: No dose adjustment (not absorbed).
hepatic: Primary use is in hepatic patients — no dose adjustment for hepatic impairment specifically; dose titrated by stool output.
ades: Abdominal cramping, bloating, flatulence, diarrhea (excessive dosing → dehydration, hypernatremia, hypokalemia; aspiration risk). Nausea/vomiting. Over-laxation can worsen HE (dehydration, hypokalemia, hypernatremia and prerenal azotemia worsen encephalopathy).
monitoring: Stool frequency/consistency (target 2–3 soft stools/day), mental status/orientation, serum electrolytes (especially Na+, K+), volume status (beware dehydration). Ammonia levels (clinical correlation — absolute value less important than trend + mental status).
ddi: Non-absorbable antibiotics (neomycin — additive NH3 reduction; historical combination now replaced by rifaximin). Antacids (may reduce lactulose bacterial fermentation). Other laxatives (additive diarrhea risk).
pearls: First-line agent for hepatic encephalopathy; rifaximin is adjunctive add-on (not monotherapy replacement). Patient adherence is a major issue (taste is very sweet/unpleasant, causes significant bloating). Individual dose titration to stool frequency is more important than fixed dosing. Over-treatment (>4 watery stools/day) causes dehydration and electrolyte disturbances that can worsen encephalopathy — educate patients/caregivers. For patients who cannot take PO (coma), rectal administration is appropriate.
trials: Sharma et al 2009 (lactulose secondary prophylaxis of HE); rifaximin + lactulose HE trial (Bass et al, NEJM 2010)
pk: NOT absorbed (poorly hydrolyzed by intestinal disaccharidases). Acts as osmotic laxative in colon. Fermented by colonic bacteria to acidic metabolites.
highyield:
• Hepatic encephalopathy: titrate dose to 2–3 soft stools/day (NOT watery diarrhea)
• Mechanism in HE: colonic acidification traps NH₃ as NH₄⁺ (non-absorbable); cathartic effect
• Hypernatremia risk with excessive use (osmotic diarrhea → free water loss)
• Diabetes: contains some galactose — monitor glucose in diabetic patients
• Palatability issues common — mix with juice; alternative formulations available

name: Sertraline
moa: Selectively inhibits serotonin transporter (SERT) → blocks reuptake of serotonin (5-HT) from synaptic cleft → increased synaptic serotonin concentrations → downregulation of postsynaptic 5-HT1A/2A receptors over 2–4 weeks (explains therapeutic delay). Minimal effect on norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake. Some sigma-1 receptor activity.
indications: Major depressive disorder (MDD); panic disorder; OCD; PTSD; social anxiety disorder; premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). First-line SSRI for most psychiatric indications. Safe in cardiac disease (SADHART trial).
dosing: MDD/anxiety: Start 25–50 mg/day PO; target 50–200 mg/day; max 200 mg/day. PMDD: 50 mg/day (cycle days 14–28 or continuously). Titrate slowly in elderly (start 25 mg, max 100 mg) — more sensitive to side effects. Increase by 25–50 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week (label); allow ~4–6 weeks at a therapeutic dose to judge response (adequate trial 8–12 weeks).
renal: No dose adjustment needed (minimal renal elimination).
hepatic: Mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh 5–6): use half the recommended starting dose and therapeutic range (increased exposure); moderate–severe impairment: not recommended.
ades: GI (N/V/D — most common early, often resolve in 2–4 weeks), sexual dysfunction (decreased libido, delayed orgasm/ejaculation — common and often persistent; use as switching consideration), weight gain (modest, long-term), insomnia or somnolence, headache, dry mouth. QTc prolongation (modest, less than TCAs). Hyponatremia (SIADH — elderly, women, low body weight). Bruising/bleeding (platelet serotonin depletion). Activation/agitation early in treatment (monitor in anxiety/suicidal patients). Serotonin syndrome (with serotonergic combinations).
monitoring: Mental status (suicidal ideation — black box warning for pediatric/young adults ≤24; assess at 1, 2, 4 weeks initially), therapeutic response assessment at 4–8 weeks, metabolic monitoring (weight, glucose), sexual function, sleep, QTc at baseline if cardiac risk factors, sodium if elderly.
ddi: MAO inhibitors (serotonin syndrome — 14-day washout required; 5 weeks for fluoxetine). Serotonergic agents (triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, linezolid — serotonin syndrome risk). NSAIDs/anticoagulants (platelet dysfunction + GI bleed risk). Pimozide (contraindicated — QT prolongation); disulfiram with oral concentrate (contraindicated — contains alcohol). Cimetidine (↑ sertraline AUC ~50% — no dose adjustment needed). CYP2D6 inhibitor (moderate) — increases levels of TCAs, antipsychotics, some beta-blockers.
pearls: Most commonly prescribed antidepressant globally. 4–6 week onset for full antidepressant effect — counsel patients about delayed response and not to discontinue prematurely. SADHART trial: sertraline safe in post-MI patients (no adverse cardiac outcomes). STAR*D trial: step-wise approach — switch or augment if inadequate response after 8–12 weeks. Discontinuation syndrome: taper gradually to avoid dizziness, paresthesias ("brain zaps"), irritability. Sertraline among the preferred SSRIs in pregnancy (risk category — some data in first trimester). SSRI choice often driven by drug interactions, patient history, and side effect profile.
trials: SADHART (post-MI depression), STAR*D (depression treatment sequence), IMPACT (late-life depression)
pk: t½ ~26 hours (intermediate among SSRIs; shorter than fluoxetine but longer than fluvoxamine/paroxetine). Metabolized by multiple CYPs (2B6, 2C19, 2C9, 2D6, 3A4) to desmethylsertraline, which is largely inactive (~1/20th potency).
bbw: SUICIDALITY: Increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults (≤24 years) with MDD and other psychiatric disorders. Monitor closely during initial treatment.
highyield:
• Most commonly prescribed SSRI — first-line for MDD, GAD, PTSD, OCD, panic disorder
• Serotonin syndrome: risk with MAOIs (contraindicated, 14-day washout), linezolid, triptans, tramadol, fentanyl
• Sexual dysfunction (decreased libido, anorgasmia) in 30–40% — counsel patients
• QTc prolongation (mild) — relevant in patients on other QT-prolonging drugs
• Avoid abrupt discontinuation: serotonin discontinuation syndrome (FINISH mnemonic)

name: Quetiapine
moa: Antagonizes multiple receptors: D2 (dopamine), 5-HT2A (serotonin), H1 (histamine — sedation), alpha-1 adrenergic (orthostatic hypotension), muscarinic (less than typical). D2 antagonism → antipsychotic effect; 5-HT2A antagonism → mood stabilization, fewer EPS; H1 antagonism → sedation (significant — often used intentionally for insomnia/anxiety). Active metabolite norquetiapine inhibits NET (antidepressant mechanism).
indications: Schizophrenia; bipolar disorder (manic, depressive, mixed episodes + maintenance); adjunctive MDD (Seroquel XR). No IM formulation exists (not used for acute IM agitation). Off-label: insomnia (low-dose 25–50 mg — widespread but controversial), dementia-related agitation (black box warning — use with caution).
dosing: Schizophrenia: start 25 mg BID, titrate to 300–400 mg/day by day 4; usual 150–750 mg/day (IR max 750 mg/day; XR 400–800 mg/day). Bipolar mania: 50 mg BID day 1 → target 400–800 mg/day by day 4. Bipolar depression: 50 mg QHS → 300 mg QHS. Adjunctive MDD: 50–300 mg/day. XR (extended-release): once daily dosing.
renal: No dose adjustment needed (minimal renal excretion).
hepatic: Start with lower doses (25 mg/day), titrate slowly — CYP3A4 metabolism reduced; increase exposure.
ades: Sedation (H1 — significant, dose-related), metabolic syndrome (weight gain, glucose dysregulation/diabetes, dyslipidemia — high risk among atypicals, behind clozapine and olanzapine), orthostatic hypotension (alpha-1), dry mouth, constipation, QTc prolongation (moderate), tardive dyskinesia (lower risk than typical antipsychotics), cataracts (FDA monitoring recommendation — slit-lamp exam at initiation and 6-month intervals), agranulocytosis (rare). BLACK BOX: increased mortality in elderly with dementia-related psychosis.
monitoring: Metabolic: weight/BMI, fasting glucose/A1c, fasting lipids at baseline then quarterly (first year), then annually. CBC if signs of infection. QTc baseline and PRN. Neurological: AIMS exam annually for tardive dyskinesia. Ophthalmology: slit-lamp lens exam at baseline and q6 months. Mental status.
ddi: protease inhibitors dramatically increase quetiapine levels (→ CNS depression, QTc prolongation, sudden death — avoid strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or reduce quetiapine dose to one-sixth of normal)
pearls: Off-label insomnia: widely prescribed at low doses (25–50 mg) but lacks rigorous trial evidence; sedation is purely H1-mediated at low doses (not therapeutic for psychosis); risk of metabolic side effects even at low doses. Metabolic monitoring is mandatory. Seroquel is the brand (generic widely available). CATIE trial: olanzapine was most effective antipsychotic but worst metabolic profile; quetiapine in the middle. For bipolar depression: quetiapine monotherapy (300 mg QHS) is FDA-approved and effective (BOLDER I/II trials — NNT ~5–7 for response).
trials: CATIE trial (Lieberman NEJM 2005), BOLDER I and II and EMBOLDEN I and II (quetiapine in bipolar depression)
pk: t½ ~6–7 h. Bioavailability ~100% (oral, food increases Cmax ~25%). Protein binding ~83%. Metabolized by CYP3A4 (primary). Active metabolite: norquetiapine (also antidepressant active).
bbw: ELDERLY DEMENTIA-RELATED PSYCHOSIS: Increased mortality with antipsychotics in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Not FDA-approved for this indication. SUICIDALITY (as adjunct for MDD): See all antidepressant BBW.
highyield:
• Atypical antipsychotic — used for schizophrenia, bipolar I & II, MDD adjunct
• Metabolic syndrome: weight gain, dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia (monitor fasting glucose, lipids, waist circumference)
• Sedation + QTc prolongation are dose-dependent side effects
• CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole): require dose reduction; inducers (phenytoin, rifampin): require dose increase ×5
• Low doses (25–100 mg) often used off-label for insomnia — evidence limited, metabolic risks persist

name: Lithium
moa: Exact mechanism incompletely understood. Proposed: inhibits inositol monophosphatase (IP1) and inositol polyphosphate 1-phosphatase → depletes inositol → reduces PKC signaling cascade; inhibits GSK-3 beta (glycogen synthase kinase) → neuroprotective; modulates G-protein signaling; increases neurotrophin BDNF. Interferes with Na+/K+ pumps and replaces Na+ in cells. Narrow therapeutic index.
indications: Bipolar disorder (gold standard for maintenance — most evidence for suicide reduction); acute mania; bipolar depression (augmentation); unipolar MDD (augmentation, treatment-resistant); schizoaffective disorder. Only drug with strong evidence for reducing suicide in bipolar and unipolar depression.
dosing: Immediate-release: 300 mg TID initially, titrate to therapeutic level. Extended-release (Lithobid): 450–900 mg BID. Target serum concentration: 0.8–1.2 mEq/L in acute mania; 0.6–1.0 mEq/L for maintenance (2024 ACCP Updates in Therapeutics, Psychiatry). Draw trough level 12h after last dose. Very weight-based and renally cleared — adjust carefully.
renal: Entirely renally cleared (competes with Na+ for tubular reabsorption — hyponatremia → lithium retention → toxicity). Current label: CrCl 30–89 mL/min — start at lower doses and titrate slowly with frequent levels; CrCl <30 — not recommended (older references: CrCl 10–50 give 50–75% of usual dose). NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, diuretics → dramatically increase lithium levels. Dehydration major toxicity risk.
hepatic: No hepatic metabolism — no hepatic adjustment needed. All clearance is renal.
ades: At therapeutic levels: fine tremor, polyuria/polydipsia (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — vasopressin-resistant), hypothyroidism (5–35% — monitor TSH), weight gain, GI upset (take with food), cognitive dulling, acne/psoriasis exacerbation, ECG changes (T-wave flattening). TOXICITY signs (levels >1.5): coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, lethargy → >2.0: nystagmus, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, irreversible neurologic damage → >2.5: renal failure, coma, death.
monitoring: Lithium level (draw 12h trough): at steady state (5 days after initiation/dose change) then q3–6 months when stable. Renal function (BUN/Cr, GFR) and electrolytes (especially Na+) q6 months. TSH q6–12 months. Calcium q6 months (lithium → hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia with chronic use). Weight. BP. Pregnancy test (teratogen — Ebstein's anomaly risk, especially first trimester).
ddi: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen → reduce renal Li+ clearance by 12–60% → toxicity). ACEi/ARBs (reduce GFR → Li+ accumulates → toxicity — AVOID; if used, reduce Li+ dose and monitor intensely). Thiazide diuretics (Na+ depletion → increased Li+ reabsorption → toxicity). Loop diuretics (safer than thiazides). Metronidazole (reduces Li+ clearance). Serotonin syndrome risk with serotoninergic drugs.
pearls: Only medication proven to reduce suicide risk in both bipolar AND unipolar depression (meta-analysis). Narrow TI — toxicity is life-threatening and can be irreversible (permanent cerebellar damage). Salt intake must be consistent — low-Na+ diet increases Li+ retention. Dehydration (vomiting/diarrhea/fever/exercise) → Li+ toxicity → HOLD lithium and aggressively hydrate. ESRD: lithium is dialyzable — HD used in severe toxicity. Lithium-induced NDI: treat with amiloride (potassium-sparing) or thiazide diuretic (paradoxical antidiuretic in NDI).
trials: Cipriani et al. Lancet 2013 (meta-analysis — lithium suicide reduction), EMBOLDEN I/II (bipolar)
pk: Complete oral absorption. NOT protein bound. NOT metabolized (excreted unchanged). t½ = 18-36h. Renal elimination (competing with Na+ reabsorption—sodium depletion increases lithium retention).
bbw: Lithium toxicity is closely related to serum lithium concentrations and can occur at doses close to therapeutic levels. Facilities for prompt and accurate serum lithium determinations should be available before initiating therapy.
highyield:
• Narrow TI: target 0.8–1.2 mEq/L in acute mania; 0.6–1.0 mEq/L for maintenance; >1.5 mEq/L = toxicity risk
• Toxicity signs: coarse tremor, confusion, ataxia, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias (fine tremor = therapeutic)
• NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs, thiazides: all increase lithium levels (reduce renal clearance) → toxicity
• Sodium depletion (low-Na diet, excessive sweating, diarrhea) increases lithium reabsorption → toxicity
• Thyroid and renal function monitoring at baseline, q6 months: hypothyroidism (~20%), nephrogenic DI

name: Ondansetron
moa: Selective competitive antagonist of serotonin 5-HT3 receptors. Chemotherapy/radiation → enterochromaffin cells in GI tract release serotonin → activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferent neurons → emesis. Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 in GI tract AND area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone) → prevents acute CINV. Limited effect on delayed CINV (different mechanism — substance P/NK1).
indications: Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) — acute phase (first 24h); radiation-induced nausea and vomiting; postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV); refractory nausea in various clinical settings. First-line antiemetic for highly/moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (combined with dexamethasone ± NK1 antagonist for highly emetogenic regimens).
dosing: CINV: 8 mg IV/PO q8h or 24 mg PO x1 before chemotherapy. PONV: 4 mg IV at end of surgery. General N/V: 4–8 mg PO/IV q4–6h PRN. ODT (orally disintegrating) useful for nauseous patients. Maximum single dose: 16 mg IV (QTc risk).
renal: No dose adjustment required (hepatically eliminated).
hepatic: Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C): do not exceed a total daily dose of 8 mg (PO or IV) (reduced clearance, t½ ~20 h).
ades: Headache, constipation, dizziness, QTc prolongation (dose-dependent), serotonin syndrome (rare, high doses + other serotonergic agents).
monitoring: QTc at baseline (if high-risk: electrolyte abnormalities, cardiac history, concurrent QTc-prolonging drugs). Electrolytes (hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia worsen QTc risk). Bowel function (constipation). Nausea/vomiting control assessment.
ddi: QTc-prolonging agents (additive risk — cardiac monitoring). Serotonin syndrome risk with linezolid, MAOIs, triptans, tramadol. Apomorphine (severe hypotension — contraindicated). CYP3A4/2D6 enzymes involved; few major clinical interactions.
pearls: 5-HT3 antagonists are the most important antiemetics for acute CINV. For highly emetogenic chemotherapy (cisplatin, doxorubicin-cyclophosphamide): triplet therapy = 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone + NK1 antagonist (aprepitant/fosaprepitant). Delayed CINV (>24h after chemo): NK1 antagonists more important (substance P/NK1 receptor-mediated). QTc 2011 FDA warning: avoid IV ondansetron in patients with congenital long QT syndrome; ensure electrolytes (K+, Mg2+) are normal. ODT dissolves on tongue — useful when patient cannot swallow. Palonosetron (Aloxi): second-gen 5-HT3 antagonist with stronger/longer binding and better delayed CINV coverage.
trials: MASCC antiemesis guideline 2023, ASCO antiemesis guidelines, Hesketh classification (emetogenicity)
pk: t½ ~3–5 h. Bioavailability ~60% (oral). Protein binding 70–76%. Metabolized by CYP3A4, CYP1A2, CYP2D6. Excretion: renal ~44% (metabolites), fecal ~25%.
highyield:
• 5-HT3 receptor antagonist — first-line antiemetic for chemotherapy-induced N/V (CINV)
• QTc prolongation: dose-dependent; IV 32 mg single dose removed from market; max IV single dose now 16 mg
• Serotonin syndrome: rare but possible with other serotonergic agents (tramadol, SSRIs)
• Headache most common ADE; constipation also common (5-HT3 blockade in GI tract)
• CYP3A4 metabolized — aprepitant/fosaprepitant combination enhances antiemetic coverage for highly emetogenic chemo

name: Filgrastim
class: G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) / myeloid growth factor
moa: Recombinant human G-CSF. Binds G-CSF receptor on neutrophil precursors → stimulates proliferation, differentiation, and survival of neutrophil progenitor cells in bone marrow → increases neutrophil production and release → raises ANC. Also activates mature neutrophils (enhances phagocytosis, antibody-dependent cytotoxicity). Shortens duration of severe neutropenia after chemotherapy.
indications: Febrile neutropenia prevention (primary/secondary prophylaxis in high-risk chemotherapy regimens); treatment of established severe neutropenia; mobilization of stem cells for HSCT (with apheresis); congenital/cyclic/idiopathic neutropenia; AML induction (post-chemo neutrophil recovery).
dosing: Myelosuppressive chemotherapy: 5 mcg/kg/day SC (or short/continuous IV infusion), starting ≥24 h after chemotherapy; continue daily for up to 2 weeks or until ANC reaches 10,000/mm³ after the expected nadir; may escalate by 5 mcg/kg per cycle. BMT: 10 mcg/kg/day IV. PBPC mobilization: 10 mcg/kg/day SC ≥4 days before first apheresis. Severe chronic neutropenia: congenital 6 mcg/kg BID; idiopathic/cyclic 5 mcg/kg daily. Do NOT administer in the period 24 hours before through 24 hours after cytotoxic chemotherapy.
renal: No dose adjustment required.
hepatic: No dose adjustment required.
ades: Bone pain (medullary pain from marrow expansion — 10–30%; treat with acetaminophen or antihistamines; NSAIDs also effective), fever, splenomegaly (rarely splenic rupture — RARE but serious: educate patients on left upper quadrant/shoulder pain → immediate evaluation), injection site reactions, leukocytosis (if ANC >10,000 → consider dose reduction/hold), thrombocytopenia, ARDS (pulmonary infiltrates with G-CSF in sepsis — caution in critically ill).
monitoring: ANC and platelets 2x/week during therapy; spleen size assessment (history of splenomegaly — periodic US); CBC prior to each dose in stem cell mobilization; vital signs.
ddi: Chemotherapy (avoid within 24h of cytotoxic chemotherapy — stimulating proliferating marrow cells during chemo increases myelosuppression). Bleomycin (pulmonary toxicity enhanced). Lithium (additive neutrophil-releasing effect — may amplify G-CSF effect).
pearls: ASCO guidelines: primary G-CSF prophylaxis recommended when febrile neutropenia risk ≥20% with planned regimen; consider at 10–20% with individual patient risk factors. Do NOT start during active infection or with cytotoxic chemo. Pegfilgrastim (Neulasta, Fulphila): long-acting G-CSF (pegylated) — single dose per chemotherapy cycle (24h after chemo); equivalent efficacy to daily filgrastim; preferred for convenience. Biosimilars (Zarxio, others) are FDA-approved and therapeutically equivalent. Bone pain management: loratadine 10 mg/day (or NSAIDs) commonly used for bone pain — supporting evidence is limited (not a formal ASCO recommendation).
trials: ASCO/NCCN G-CSF guidelines, multiple RCTs establishing febrile neutropenia risk reduction
pk: t½ ~3.5 h (SC). Bioavailability ~60–70% (SC). Not protein-bound significantly. Eliminated by receptor-mediated clearance (neutrophil-dependent) and renal clearance.
highyield:
• G-CSF — stimulates neutrophil production; used for febrile neutropenia prophylaxis and treatment
• ASCO/NCCN guidelines: primary prophylaxis if chemotherapy regimen has ≥20% febrile neutropenia risk
• Do NOT give 24 h before or 24 h after myelosuppressive chemotherapy (bone marrow sensitization)
• Bone pain most common side effect (marrow expansion) — ibuprofen or loratadine may help
• Zarxio (filgrastim-sndz): FDA-approved biosimilar; not automatically interchangeable at all pharmacies without prescriber approval

name: Tacrolimus
moa: Binds FK506-binding protein 12 (FKBP12) → tacrolimus-FKBP12 complex inhibits calcineurin phosphatase → prevents dephosphorylation of NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells) → blocks IL-2 gene transcription → impairs T-cell activation and proliferation. 100x more potent than cyclosporine per unit mass.
indications: Solid organ transplant rejection prophylaxis (kidney, liver, heart, lung, pancreas — first-line CNI); treatment of acute cellular rejection; graft-vs-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis in HSCT; topical use (Protopic) for atopic dermatitis.
dosing: Highly variable — individualized by TDM. Kidney transplant: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg/day PO in 2 divided doses (IR) initially; target trough per protocol (label kidney: 7–20 ng/mL months 1–3 then 5–15 ng/mL with azathioprine; 4–11 ng/mL with MMF + IL-2RA; many centers ~8–12 early, 5–10 maintenance). Liver transplant: similar. Highly variable absorption — TDM is MANDATORY. Astagraf XL / Envarsus XR (once daily, extended-release): NOT interchangeable with IR (Envarsus conversion = 80% of IR total daily dose); may improve adherence.
renal: Nephrotoxic — careful TDM essential. In impaired renal function from tacrolimus toxicity, dose reduction and level monitoring required. CKD itself doesn't change dose requirements; monitor trough levels.
hepatic: Severe hepatic impairment: reduced metabolism → higher levels. Start at lower end, increase TDM frequency. CYP3A4/5 metabolized.
ades: Nephrotoxicity (dose-dependent, chronic — major long-term concern; both acute functional and chronic fibrotic nephropathy), neurotoxicity (tremor, headache, paresthesias, seizures, PRES — posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome), hypertension, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, new-onset diabetes after transplant (NODAT — worse than cyclosporine), infections (BK virus nephropathy, CMV, fungal — immunosuppression), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, GI disturbance, alopecia. No gingival hyperplasia/hirsutism (advantage over cyclosporine).
monitoring: MANDATORY trough levels (draw 12h post-dose IR, 24h post-dose XL) at each clinic visit initially, then q1–3 months when stable. SCr/GFR, electrolytes (K+, Mg2+), glucose/A1c (NODAT screening), CBC, BP, magnesium (hypoMg common, requires supplementation). BK virus PCR in kidney transplant. CMV PCR in high-risk patients.
ddi: Major CYP3A4/P-gp substrate — EXTENSIVE interactions. Strong inhibitors (azoles, diltiazem, verapamil, macrolides, ritonavir) → 2–10x increase in tacrolimus levels → toxicity. Strong inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's Wort) → dramatic reduction in levels → rejection risk. Grapefruit juice (CYP3A4 inhibition) — AVOID. NSAIDs (additive nephrotoxicity). Potassium-sparing diuretics (additive hyperkalemia). Sirolimus (additive nephrotoxicity — avoid concurrent use in most protocols).
pearls: Narrow therapeutic index — TDM mandatory for all patients. Generic tacrolimus substitution is controversial — FDA considers bioequivalent but transplant societies recommend AGAINST switching formulations without dose adjustment and increased monitoring (risk of rejection or toxicity). NODAT (new-onset diabetes after transplant) is significantly more common with tacrolimus than cyclosporine. PRES is a serious CNS complication — headache, seizures, visual disturbance, altered mental status + hypertension → brain MRI → tacrolimus reduction/discontinuation. BK nephropathy: surveillance PCR + reduce immunosuppression is treatment.
trials: US Renal Transplant Study (tacrolimus vs. cyclosporine), SYMPHONY trial, ELITE-Symphony
pk: t½ ~12 h (variable). Bioavailability ~20–25% (oral, highly variable); food reduces absorption. Protein binding >99% (RBC, albumin). Metabolized by CYP3A4/3A5 (major). Excretion: fecal ~92%.
bbw: MALIGNANCIES AND SERIOUS INFECTIONS: increased risk of serious infections and malignancies (lymphoma, skin cancer) that may lead to hospitalization or death; prescribe only by physicians experienced in immunosuppression/transplant. Astagraf XL additionally: INCREASED MORTALITY IN FEMALE LIVER TRANSPLANT PATIENTS — not approved for liver transplant. (Non-interchangeability of IR/XR products is a Warning/Precaution on medication errors, not boxed.)
highyield:
• Calcineurin inhibitor — inhibits IL-2 production → T-cell suppression
• Narrow TI: TDM critical; troughs vary by indication/regimen (label: kidney 7–20 ng/mL months 1–3 with azathioprine or 4–11 with MMF; liver 5–20 ng/mL)
• CYP3A4 and P-gp: extensive DDIs — azole antifungals, macrolides, diltiazem ↑ levels; rifampin, phenytoin ↓ levels
• Nephrotoxicity (acute and chronic), neurotoxicity (tremor, PRES), hyperglycemia (NODAT), hyperkalemia, hypertension
• CYP3A5 polymorphism: extensive metabolizers require higher doses; genotyping can guide initial dosing

name: Mycophenolate Mofetil / Mycophenolic Acid
moa: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is a prodrug hydrolyzed to mycophenolic acid (MPA). MPA selectively inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) — rate-limiting enzyme in de novo purine (guanosine) synthesis. Lymphocytes rely predominantly on de novo pathway (unlike other cells that use salvage pathway) → selective antiproliferative effect on T and B lymphocytes → reduced antibody production and cell-mediated immunity.
indications: Solid organ transplant rejection prophylaxis (kidney, liver, heart — first-line antiproliferative agent replacing azathioprine); lupus nephritis; IgA nephropathy; ANCA-associated vasculitis; myasthenia gravis. Combined with tacrolimus and corticosteroids as standard triple therapy in renal transplant.
dosing: Kidney transplant: 1000 mg PO/IV BID (MMF; heart/liver 1500 mg BID) or 720 mg BID (enteric-coated MPA — Myfortic). Adjust for GI intolerance (reduce dose). Doses given on empty stomach for MPA (or with food if GI intolerant for MMF). NOT interchangeable mg-for-mg (Myfortic 720 mg = CellCept 1000 mg).
renal: Kidney transplant patients with severe chronic graft impairment (GFR <25 mL/min/1.73 m²) outside the immediate post-transplant period: do not exceed 1 g BID; no adjustment for delayed graft function post-op (monitor). MPA glucuronide (MPAG) accumulates in renal impairment.
hepatic: No dose adjustment for hepatic impairment alone.
ades: GI dominant: diarrhea (most common — dose-dependent, use Myfortic EC for better GI tolerability), nausea/vomiting/cramping, GI ulceration/bleeding. Myelosuppression: leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia (CBC monitoring). Infections (increased risk — CMV, BK virus, PCP, fungal). Teratogenicity (Category D — absolute contraindication in pregnancy; effective contraception MANDATORY; REMS program for women of childbearing potential). Lymphoma/malignancy risk with long-term immunosuppression.
monitoring: CBC with differential weekly for month 1, twice monthly for months 2–3, then monthly through the first year (myelosuppression monitoring). CMV PCR in at-risk patients. Pregnancy tests + contraception counseling (REMS). Diarrhea severity (consider dose reduction or switch to enteric-coated Myfortic). MPA levels (optional — target AUC 30–60 mg·h/L; not universally performed but used in rejection/toxicity situations).
ddi: Antacids/PPIs (reduce MMF absorption — separate by 2h from antacids). Cholestyramine/colestipol (interrupt enterohepatic recirculation → reduce MPA levels by 40%). Azathioprine (do NOT combine — additive myelosuppression). Rifampin (reduces MPA levels via enterohepatic recirculation disruption). Sevelamer (reduces MPA levels — separate administration). Oral contraceptives (slightly reduced efficacy — use additional contraceptive method).
pearls: Myfortic (enteric-coated MPA) causes less GI side effects vs. CellCept — switch if diarrhea is problematic (NOT bioequivalent mg-for-mg; Myfortic 720 = CellCept 1000). REMS program (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) for MMF due to teratogenicity — mandatory counseling. Stop mycophenolate ≥6 weeks before planned conception (label: contraception until 6 weeks after stopping; male patients: condoms during and 90 days after; many transplant programs switch to azathioprine ~3 months ahead). MMF replaced azathioprine as antiproliferative in most transplant regimens due to superior rejection prevention. MPA levels: TDM available but limited evidence that AUC-guided dosing improves outcomes vs. fixed dosing.
trials: Sollinger NEJM 1995 (MMF vs. azathioprine), Symphony trial, MYSS trial
pk: MMF (CellCept) → MPA (active) by esterases; MPA t½ ~18 h. Bioavailability MMF ~94%; MPA (Myfortic) ~72%. Protein binding >97%. Enterohepatic recycling (UGT1A9). Excretion: renal ~93% (MPAG).
bbw: EMBRYO-FETAL TOXICITY: Do not use in pregnancy; causes miscarriage and birth defects. REMS program required. Malignancy and serious infections.
highyield:
• Inhibits IMPDH → blocks purine synthesis → antiproliferative for T and B lymphocytes
• MMF and MPA (sodium) are NOT interchangeable (different salt forms, different bioavailability) — DO NOT substitute without dose adjustment
• GI toxicity (diarrhea, N/V) dose-limiting — enteric-coated MPA (Myfortic) may reduce GI effects
• REMS program required — pregnancy testing and acceptable contraception (IUD/sterilization alone, or two methods) in females of reproductive potential
• Azathioprine alternative: less effective but fewer GI effects; XO inhibitor allopurinol dramatically ↑ azathioprine toxicity (AVOID combination)

name: Morphine
moa: Binds mu-opioid receptors (MOR) predominantly → G-protein (Gi/o) coupling → decreased cAMP, increased K+ conductance (hyperpolarization), decreased Ca2+ entry → reduced neuronal excitability → analgesic, euphoric, sedating effects. Also delta and kappa receptor activity. Central and peripheral (dorsal horn) action. Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G) is active, potent metabolite — accumulates in renal failure.
indications: Management of acute pain severe enough to require an opioid when alternatives are inadequate (IR); ER (MS Contin, Kadian): severe and persistent pain requiring an extended-period opioid that cannot be adequately treated with alternatives (not for PRN use). acute MI pain (IV morphine — but ATLANTIC and IMPRESSION data show morphine delays/attenuates oral P2Y12 inhibitor absorption/effect)
dosing: Opioid-naive adults: 2.5–5 mg IV q4h PRN; 15–30 mg PO q4h (IR). Chronic pain: titrate ER formulation (MS Contin) with IR breakthrough dosing (10–15% of total daily dose for breakthrough). PCA: 1–2 mg demand dose with 6–10 min lockout. Elderly/renal: reduce dose, increase interval. Equianalgesic table: morphine 10 mg IV = 30 mg PO (3:1 oral:IV ratio).
renal: Active metabolite M6G accumulates in CKD/ESRD → prolonged sedation, respiratory depression. Use with extreme caution in GFR <30; prefer alternative opioids (hydromorphone, fentanyl) in ESRD.
hepatic: Hepatic metabolism (glucuronidation — relatively preserved vs. CYP-dependent drugs). Reduce dose in severe cirrhosis (reduced first-pass metabolism → increased bioavailability PO, decreased clearance).
ades: Respiratory depression (most feared — dose-dependent; reversal with naloxone 0.4 mg IV q2–3 min up to 10 mg), constipation (most common long-term — tolerance does NOT develop; always prescribe bowel regimen), N/V (common early, tolerance develops), sedation, pruritus (histamine release — treat with hydroxyzine not diphenhydramine), urinary retention (alpha tone in sphincter), physical dependence/withdrawal, tolerance, addiction risk, hyperalgesia (paradoxical — chronic opioids can worsen pain sensitivity), immunosuppression (chronic).
monitoring: Pain score (NRS 0–10), respiratory rate/depth, sedation scale (RASS, Pasero), constipation, PDMP (prescription drug monitoring program) check before prescribing, ORT (Opioid Risk Tool) for abuse potential, tolerance signs, COWS (clinical opioid withdrawal scale if tapering).
ddi: CNS depressants (benzodiazepines — additive respiratory depression: BLACK BOX warning FDA 2016; benzodiazepines are involved in a substantial share (~30%) of opioid overdose deaths), alcohol, muscle relaxants. MAOIs (contraindicated — severe, unpredictable reactions). Serotonergic agents (serotonin syndrome). Not CYP-dependent (UGT2B7) — CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers affect related opioids (oxycodone, fentanyl), not morphine.
pearls: Morphine is the prototype opioid — all others are compared to it (equianalgesic table). AVOID in ESRD (M6G accumulation). Respiratory depression reversal: naloxone 0.04–0.4 mg IV (titrate low in opioid-tolerant patients to avoid precipitating withdrawal). Constipation: prescribe osmotic laxative (PEG/lactulose) or peripheral mu-opioid receptor antagonist (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol) routinely — tolerance never develops to constipation. CDC 2022 guideline: prescribe lowest effective dose of IR opioids, no greater quantity than needed for the expected duration of severe pain (the 2016 '≤3 days' numeric limit was removed), use non-opioid analgesia as first-line. Risk mitigation: naloxone co-prescribing for all patients on long-term opioids or high doses.
trials: CDC Opioid Prescribing Guidelines 2022, SPACE trial (opioids vs. non-opioids for chronic musculoskeletal pain)
pk: t½ ~2–4 h. Bioavailability PO ~20–40% (first-pass — significant). Protein binding ~35%. Metabolized by UGT2B7 → M6G (active, potent), M3G (neuroexcitatory). Excretion: renal (90% M3G + M6G).
bbw: ADDICTION, ABUSE, and MISUSE: High abuse potential. LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION (ER: swallow whole — crushing/chewing causes rapid release of a potentially fatal dose). ACCIDENTAL INGESTION (fatal, especially children). NEONATAL OPIOID WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME. RISKS FROM CONCOMITANT USE WITH BENZODIAZEPINES OR OTHER CNS DEPRESSANTS (including alcohol). OPIOID ANALGESIC REMS. (No CYP450 boxed warning — morphine is glucuronidated, unlike oxycodone/fentanyl/hydrocodone.)
highyield: • Titrate to effect: for uncontrolled severe pain in opioid-naive patients, reassess and increase the dose ~25–50% with close monitoring for sedation and respiratory depression

name: Naloxone
moa: Competitive antagonist at mu, delta, and kappa opioid receptors with high affinity (higher than most agonists) → rapidly displaces opioids → reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression, sedation, analgesia, and miosis within 1–2 min IV. Short duration (30–90 min IV) — shorter than most opioids → RE-SEDATION IS A MAJOR RISK.
indications: Opioid overdose (life-threatening respiratory depression) — IV/IM/intranasal/SC. Community distribution (Narcan nasal spray) for layperson use. Intraoperative opioid reversal. Pruritus reversal (low doses). Opioid-induced constipation is treated with peripherally-acting derivatives (naloxegol = PEGylated naloxone; methylnaltrexone is a separate PAMORA), not naloxone itself.
dosing: Opioid overdose: 0.4–2 mg IV/IM/SC q2–3 min up to 10 mg (if no response after 10 mg, reconsider opioid diagnosis). Intranasal (Narcan): 4 mg = one spray in ONE nostril; if no response or relapse, repeat q2–3 min with a new device in the alternate nostril (Kloxxado 8 mg; RiVive 3 mg). POST-REVERSAL: duration shorter than most opioids → may need repeat doses, continuous infusion (2/3 of effective bolus dose per hour), or prolonged monitoring (4–6h for short-acting; 12–24h for long-acting opioids/methadone). Opioid-tolerant patients: use lowest effective dose (0.04 mg titrated) to avoid precipitating acute withdrawal.
renal: No dose adjustment needed.
hepatic: No dose adjustment needed; primarily hepatically metabolized (glucuronidation).
ades: In opioid-naive: no significant effects. In opioid-tolerant/dependent: precipitates ACUTE OPIOID WITHDRAWAL — agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, N/V/D, pain crisis. Pulmonary edema (rare — likely mechanism sympathetic surge after reversal). Ventricular arrhythmias (tachycardia, VF — rare with rapid large doses).
monitoring: Respiratory rate (primary endpoint — target >8–10 breaths/min, adequate depth), oxygen saturation (SpO2), level of consciousness, heart rate and BP. Watch for RE-NARCOTIZATION (return of respiratory depression as naloxone wears off): typically 30–90 min. Duration of monitoring depends on opioid duration/formulation.
ddi: No significant drug interactions with non-opioid drugs. Buprenorphine: high receptor affinity — requires larger naloxone doses (often 2–10 mg) to displace. Methadone: very long duration → extended naloxone monitoring/infusion needed.
pearls: Single most important concept: naloxone duration is SHORTER than most opioids — re-narcotization is common. For methadone or extended-release opioid overdose: MUST monitor for ≥12–24h and likely need repeat doses or infusion. Community naloxone access (Narcan nasal spray, Kloxxado): OTC availability since 2023; FDA (2020) labeling: discuss naloxone with all patients prescribed opioids and consider prescribing for those at increased risk; CDC 2022: offer naloxone when overdose risk is increased (e.g., ≥50 MME/day, concurrent benzodiazepines, history of overdose/OUD). Intranasal naloxone for laypersons: 4 mg (one spray, one nostril) → call 911 → repeat with new device in other nostril if no response. Buprenorphine/naloxone (Suboxone) is a treatment for opioid use disorder — the naloxone component prevents IV misuse (precipitates withdrawal if injected IV, inactive when taken sublingually).
trials: CONSORT study (naloxone community distribution), FDA OTC approval 2023, CDC Opioid Guidelines 2022
pk: t½ ~1–2 h (IV). Bioavailability intranasal ~44–46%; IM ~65–75%. NOT orally bioavailable (extensive first-pass). Hepatic metabolism. Excretion: renal.
highyield: • Precipitates acute withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients (agitation, HTN, tachycardia, diaphoresis, N/V/diarrhea, myalgias)

name: Mesalamine (5-ASA)
moa: Topical anti-inflammatory in colonic mucosa. Inhibits prostaglandin synthesis, leukotriene production, and NF-κB activation locally.
indications: Mild-moderate ulcerative colitis (induction and maintenance). Crohn disease colitis (limited evidence).
pk: Oral formulations vary by release mechanism (pH-dependent, time-release). Local action in colon (systemic absorption minimized). Rectal forms (suppositories, enemas) for distal UC.
dosing: Induction: 2.4-4.8g/day oral. Maintenance: 1.6-2.4g/day. Rectal: mesalamine enema 4g/60mL nightly (left-sided) or suppository 1g/day (proctitis).
renal: Use with caution; evaluate renal function before starting and periodically; avoid in severe renal impairment (some products not recommended). Nephrotoxicity (interstitial nephritis) is idiosyncratic, not clearly dose-related.
hepatic: No dose adjustment needed.
ades: GI (nausea, diarrhea), headache, rash. Rare: interstitial nephritis (idiosyncratic, not dose-related; check SCr/UA), myocarditis, pancreatitis. Paradoxical flare possible.
monitoring: SCr/BMP at baseline and annually. UA for nephrotoxicity monitoring.
ddi: Azathioprine: may increase myelotoxicity. Warfarin: minor interaction.
pearls: First-line for mild-moderate UC. Rectal formulations superior for distal disease/proctitis. Check SCr/UA annually for nephrotoxicity. Not effective for luminal Crohn disease. Sulfasalazine = sulfapyridine (absorbed, causes ADRs) + 5-ASA (active).
highyield:
• First-line mild-moderate UC (induction + maintenance)
• Monitor renal function annually (interstitial nephritis)
• Rectal route preferred for distal UC/proctitis
• Sulfasalazine: sulfa-related ADRs (hemolysis in G6PD, folic acid antagonism)

name: Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine
moa: Prodrug AZA → 6-MP (non-enzymatic, glutathione); 6-MP converted to active 6-thioguanine nucleotides (6-TGN) via HGPRT, while TPMT (→ 6-MMP) and xanthine oxidase (→ 6-thiouric acid) divert it to inactive/hepatotoxic metabolites. 6-TGN inhibits purine synthesis → lymphocyte apoptosis. Onset 3-6 months.
indications: IBD (Crohn, UC) maintenance; prevention of rejection in organ transplant; autoimmune hepatitis; rheumatoid arthritis.
pk: AZA → 6-MP (intestinal wall and liver). 6-MP → 6-TGN (active) via HPRT or → 6-MMPR (hepatotoxic, inactive) via TPMT. TPMT polymorphism determines toxicity risk.
dosing: AZA: 2-3 mg/kg/day for IBD. 6-MP: 1-1.5 mg/kg/day. Start low, titrate over months.
renal: Reduce dose with renal impairment.
hepatic: Elevated 6-MMPR metabolites in liver injury → hepatotoxicity risk.
ades: Myelosuppression (dose-dependent), nausea, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis (early, usually within 30 days), increased infection risk, lymphoma risk (long-term; incl. HSTCL with TNF-inhibitor combination), non-melanoma skin cancer.
monitoring: TPMT and NUDT15 genotype or phenotype before initiation (both predict severe myelosuppression risk). CBC with platelets weekly for month 1, twice monthly for months 2–3, then monthly (or more often with dose changes); LFTs; amylase/lipase if abdominal pain.
ddi: Allopurinol: inhibits xanthine oxidase → dramatic increase in 6-MP toxicity (reduce AZA/6-MP to ~1/3–1/4 of usual dose); febuxostat — not recommended. Aminosalicylates: inhibit TPMT → increase 6-TGN (myelotoxicity).
bbw: AZA (Imuran): MALIGNANCY — chronic immunosuppression increases risk of malignancy, including post-transplant lymphoma and hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (HSTCL) in IBD patients; physicians should be familiar with this risk, the mutagenic potential, and possible hematologic toxicities. (Serious infections are a Warning, not boxed; 6-MP has no boxed warning.)
pearls: TPMT testing before initiation. Normal TPMT: standard dose. Intermediate (TPMT or NUDT15): start at 30–80% of normal dose (CPIC). Poor metabolizer: use an alternative agent for non-malignant conditions, or ~10% of normal dose given 3x/week for malignancy (severe myelosuppression). Allopurinol interaction is life-threatening.
highyield:
• TPMT phenotype MUST be checked before starting (poor metabolizer → fatal myelosuppression)
• Allopurinol + AZA/6-MP = severe toxicity (75% dose reduction required)
• Onset of IBD effect: 3-6 months (not for acute flares)
• BBW (AZA): malignancy (post-transplant lymphoma, HSTCL) — serious infections are a Warning, not boxed

name: Methylprednisolone
moa: Binds intracellular glucocorticoid receptor → translocates to nucleus → modulates gene transcription. Suppresses NF-κB, reduces inflammatory cytokines, inhibits phospholipase A2.
indications: Acute asthma/COPD exacerbation, allergic reactions, anaphylaxis, MS relapse, transplant rejection, septic shock (low-dose steroids — hydrocortisone is the agent used, not methylprednisolone), spinal cord injury (no longer recommended), IBD flare.
pk: IV/oral/IM. Oral bioavailability ~88%. t½ plasma 3.5h; biologic t½ 18-36h. Extensive hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4). Lower protein binding than prednisone.
dosing: Acute asthma: 40-80mg IV/oral daily. MS relapse: 1g IV daily x3-5 days. Transplant rejection: 500-1000mg IV. Dose equivalent: methylprednisolone 4mg = prednisone 5mg = hydrocortisone 20mg.
renal: No dose adjustment required.
hepatic: Reduced metabolism in severe liver disease; monitor for increased effects.
ades: Hyperglycemia, hypertension, fluid retention, insomnia, mood changes, HPA suppression (>3 weeks use), osteoporosis, avascular necrosis, cataracts, immunosuppression, Cushing syndrome (chronic).
monitoring: Blood glucose (especially diabetics), blood pressure, electrolytes. Bone density if long-term.
ddi: CYP3A4 inhibitors (azole antifungals, macrolides) increase levels. CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin) decrease levels. Warfarin: variable effect. NSAIDs: additive GI risk.
pearls: No HPA suppression with <3 weeks use at most doses. For septic shock: hydrocortisone 200mg/day IV (not methylprednisolone per ADRENAL/APROCCHSS trials). Pulse steroids (1g) for transplant rejection, MS relapse. ARDS: 2024 ATS and SCCM guidelines conditionally recommend corticosteroids (e.g., methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day with taper [Meduri] or dexamethasone per DEXA-ARDS, which showed benefit in moderate–severe ARDS).
highyield:
• Dose equivalences: 4mg methyl = 5mg pred = 20mg hydrocort = 0.75mg dexameth
• Septic shock: hydrocortisone 200mg/day preferred (not methylprednisolone)
• HPA suppression: avoid abrupt discontinuation after >3 weeks use
• No longer recommended for acute spinal cord injury (NASCIS benefits were post hoc subgroup findings; harms ↑ — AANS/CNS recommends against)

name: Montelukast
moa: Selectively antagonizes cysteinyl leukotriene receptor CysLT1, blocking LTC4, LTD4, LTE4. Reduces bronchoconstriction, eosinophilic inflammation, and mucus secretion.
indications: Asthma prophylaxis (mild persistent or add-on), exercise-induced bronchospasm, allergic rhinitis, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD).
pk: Rapid oral absorption; peak 3-4h. t½ = 2.7-5.5h. Extensive hepatic metabolism (CYP2C8/3A4). >99% protein bound. No renal adjustment.
dosing: Adults: 10mg once daily (evening preferred). 6-14y: 5mg. 2-5y: 4mg chewable.
renal: No dose adjustment needed.
hepatic: Use with caution in severe hepatic impairment.
ades: Generally well tolerated. Neuropsychiatric events (depression, suicidal ideation, behavioral changes — FDA BBW 2020), headache, upper respiratory infections, abdominal pain.
monitoring: Monitor for neuropsychiatric symptoms; discontinue if behavioral changes occur.
ddi: CYP inducers (rifampin, phenobarbital) may decrease montelukast levels. Generally minimal DDI profile.
bbw: Serious neuropsychiatric events including agitation, aggression, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbances, hallucinations, suicidal thinking and behavior (including completed suicide). Reserve use for allergic rhinitis patients with inadequate response or intolerance to alternative therapies; in asthma/EIB, consider benefits vs risks before prescribing.
pearls: FDA 2020 BBW added for neuropsychiatric events. Now: restrict use to patients where other therapies inadequate for allergic rhinitis (asthma: still acceptable add-on). Particularly useful as add-on in AERD (leukotriene overproduction). Not for acute bronchospasm.
highyield:
• FDA 2020 BBW: neuropsychiatric events (depression, suicidality)
• Useful add-on for aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD) — not monotherapy drug of choice
• Not for acute bronchospasm relief (no beta-agonist activity)
• Added-on value in eosinophilic asthma and exercise-induced bronchospasm

name: Acetazolamide
moa: Inhibits carbonic anhydrase in renal proximal tubule → decreased HCO3 reabsorption → bicarbonate diuresis → metabolic acidosis → compensatory increase in respiratory drive.
indications: Glaucoma (chronic open-angle, secondary, and preoperative acute angle-closure); edema due to HF or drug-induced (adjunct); centrencephalic epilepsies; prevention/amelioration of acute mountain sickness. Off-label: metabolic alkalosis (corrects alkalosis by inducing a mild hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis via bicarbonate diuresis), idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
pk: Well absorbed orally; t½ = 4-8h (extended release 10-15h). Renal elimination unchanged.
dosing: Altitude sickness: prevention 125 mg BID starting the day before ascent; treatment 250 mg BID. Glaucoma: 250mg QID or 500mg SR BID. Metabolic alkalosis: 250-500mg q6-12h IV.
renal: Avoid if CrCl <10 mL/min (ineffective + hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis risk).
hepatic: Contraindicated in cirrhosis/marked hepatic disease (alkaline urine reduces NH4+ excretion → hyperammonemia → hepatic encephalopathy).
ades: Metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, paresthesias (tingling of extremities — sulfona-mide effect), nephrolithiasis (urine alkalinization), sulfonamide hypersensitivity (cross-reactivity).
monitoring: Serum electrolytes (K+, HCO3), renal function.
ddi: Phenytoin: ↑ phenytoin levels and ↑ osteomalacia risk. Lithium: decreased tubular reabsorption (lower lithium levels). Aspirin: can cause aspirin toxicity (reduces excretion).
pearls: Contraindicated with hepatic failure (ammonia accumulation). Paresthesias are common and benign. Cross-reactivity with sulfonamide allergy (caution). Best evidence for altitude sickness prophylaxis (starts 24-48h before ascent).
highyield:
• Works for altitude sickness by causing mild metabolic acidosis → increased ventilation
• Paresthesias (tingling) are common, benign side effect from CA inhibition
• Avoid in hepatic failure (ammonia accumulation → encephalopathy)
• Sulfonamide cross-reactivity: use with caution in sulfa allergy

name: Erlotinib
moa: Reversibly inhibits EGFR (HER1) tyrosine kinase, blocking downstream MAPK/PI3K/Akt signaling, reducing cell proliferation.
indications: NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R mutation. Pancreatic cancer (in combination with gemcitabine).
pk: Oral bioavailability ~60% fasted, increased to nearly 100% with food (hence dose on an empty stomach to avoid excess exposure/toxicity). t½ = 36h.
dosing: NSCLC: 150mg once daily on empty stomach. Pancreatic cancer: 100mg/day with gemcitabine.
renal: No formal adjustment; use caution with severe renal impairment.
hepatic: No specific dose reduction; hepatic impairment (total bilirubin >ULN or Child-Pugh A, B, C): monitor closely (extra caution if bilirubin >3× ULN); interrupt or discontinue for severe changes in liver function (e.g., bilirubin >3× ULN and/or transaminases >5× ULN with normal baseline).
ades: Acneiform/papulopustular rash (70-80% — correlates with response!), diarrhea, mucositis, fatigue. Interstitial lung disease (ILD, rare, ~1% — can be fatal). Hypomagnesemia.
monitoring: LFTs (hepatotoxicity risk), monitor for ILD (new dyspnea, cough, fever). Monitor skin rash as predictor of response.
ddi: CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin) reduce erlotinib levels significantly; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors ↑ levels (reduce dose if toxicity). Cigarette smoking (CYP1A2 induction) ↓ exposure 50–60% — advise cessation; cautious dose increase if still smoking. PPI and H2-blockers reduce absorption (pH-dependent). Warfarin: INR changes (CYP2C9).
pearls: Now largely replaced by osimertinib (3rd gen EGFR TKI) for EGFR-mutated NSCLC. Rash severity correlates with treatment response (paradoxically, worse rash = better outcome). ILD requires immediate discontinuation. Avoid PPIs if possible.
highyield:
• EGFR exon 19 del or L858R = required biomarker for use
• Acneiform rash in ~75% (correlates with response—do not dose-reduce for rash alone)
• ILD (~1%): discontinue immediately if suspected
• Take on EMPTY stomach; PPIs reduce absorption

name: Levonorgestrel (Emergency Contraception)
moa: Primarily inhibits or delays ovulation. May also prevent fertilization. Does NOT prevent implantation of a fertilized egg (no abortifacient effect if already pregnant).
indications: Emergency contraception: reduces pregnancy risk after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure.
pk: Rapid oral absorption. t½ = 24-32h. Hepatic metabolism. No significant DDI at single dose.
dosing: Plan B: 1.5mg single oral dose as soon as possible, within 72 hours (effective up to 120 hours, decreasing efficacy with time). Take any time in menstrual cycle.
renal: No adjustment needed for single dose.
hepatic: Single dose well tolerated even with hepatic impairment.
ades: Menstrual changes (heavier/lighter, earlier/later menses — most common), nausea, lower abdominal pain, fatigue, headache, dizziness, breast tenderness, vomiting. Menstrual cycle may be early or late.
monitoring: Pregnancy test if next menses >1 week late. No lab monitoring needed.

Weight: may be less effective with BMI ≥30 (data conflicting; FDA did not change labeling); copper IUD (>99% effective up to 5 days) or ulipristal preferred for higher BMI. Does NOT affect existing pregnancy. OTC in all states.
